text:
Nightpeak Energy has completed the 150MW Bocanova 2 battery storage facility in south-east Texas, US, raising the total storage capacity at the Bocanova site to 300MW.

The company also announced the successful financial close for the facility, noting that it went into commercial service on 17 September.

Bocanova 2 aims to provide additional flexibility to the Electric Reliability Council of Texas electricity grid amid rising demand, particularly as data centres and other large energy consumers expand operations in the state.

Located in Brazoria County, near the Houston metropolitan area, Bocanova 2 follows Bocanova 1, an earlier 150MW battery storage project at the same site.

According to Nightpeak Energy, Bocanova 1 commenced commercial operation in August 2025.

The combined projects form part of the company’s ongoing battery storage development in a region recognised for its fast-growing power demand.

Bocanova 2 is equipped with Tesla’s Megapack 2 XL lithium-ion battery systems. It operates under a long-term offtake agreement with an investment-grade counterparty.

The financing structure included a tax equity bridge loan and a construction-to-term loan provided by MUFG Bank, while U.S. Bank supplied traditional tax equity for the project.

Nightpeak Energy co-founder and CEO/chief development officer Paris Hays said: “We are seeing large loads come to the grid at a pace and scale that is fundamentally changing how the power sector plans for new demand.

“Texas is at the forefront of that growth, and meeting it will require significant new infrastructure as well as resources that can respond quickly as conditions change.

“With 300MW now operating at Bocanova, we are putting that kind of flexibility to work in one of the most dynamic power markets in the country.”

Nightpeak Energy was founded in 2022. Since then, the company has developed and acquired more than 1GW of operating and de-risked capacity, including battery storage, gas-fired generation and powered land development.

The company continues to develop additional flexible generation and large-load projects as part of efforts to address growing power needs in the US.

title: Hyundai Motor expands India hub with Pune plant, EV push, 20.7t won investment
description:
The new Pune plant was created by Hyundai Motor in 2023 through the acquisition and expansion of the General Motors (GM) plant in Talegaon, Maharashtra, in west-central India.
Adding Kia's Anantapur plant's annual capacity (431,000 vehicles) brings Hyundai Motor Group's capacity this year to 1,425,000 vehicles per year.
Hyundai Motor plans to have the new Pune plant handle production of the local strategic model Venue, while pursuing a full electric vehicle (EV) transition at the existing Chennai plant.
Hyundai Motor Group Chair Chung Eui-sun said at the completion ceremony, "From the first time we entered India 30 years ago, Hyundai Motor worked to earn the trust of local customers.
Attending the ceremony were Chair Chung; Vice Chair Chang Jae-hoon; Hyundai Motor CEO (president) José Muñoz; and Tarun Garg, CEO of Hyundai Motor India Ltd. (HMIL), among other top executives.
text:
Hyundai Motor(313,500 won ▼ 1,500 -0.48%) said on the 14th that it held a completion ceremony for its new Pune plant in India. It is the third foothold secured about 30 years after establishing its India subsidiary in May 1996. Hyundai Motor plans to make India a pillar of future growth by using the new plant as a base to convert locally produced models to electric vehicles, and by investing in Autonomous Driving and future mobility.

The new Pune plant was created by Hyundai Motor in 2023 through the acquisition and expansion of the General Motors (GM) plant in Talegaon, Maharashtra, in west-central India. The amount Hyundai Motor invested to rebuild the plant, which began operating in 2008, into a smart manufacturing hub comes to about 1 trillion won.

The site alone is 1.2 ㎢ (about 360,000 pyeong), with an annual production capacity of 170,000 vehicles. Hyundai Motor plans to increase capacity to 250,000 by 2028 and 320,000 by 2030. Hyundai Motor estimates that the number of employees who will work at the plant will reach more than 4,700, and that the employment effect, including partner companies, will be more than 12,400.

With the start-up of the new Pune plant, Hyundai Motor has secured an annual production capacity close to 1 million vehicles when combined with the Chennai Plants 1 and 2 (824,000 vehicles per year). Adding Kia's Anantapur plant's annual capacity (431,000 vehicles) brings Hyundai Motor Group's capacity this year to 1,425,000 vehicles per year. Hyundai Motor also set a goal of raising the India subsidiary's export share to 30% by 2030.

The first mass-produced model at the new Pune plant is the subcompact sport utility vehicle (SUV) All New Venue. In addition to domestic sales in India, it will also build units for export to more than 30 countries worldwide, including Mexico, Chile, South Africa and Saudi Arabia. Hyundai Motor plans to expand mass-produced models to include hybrid vehicles (HEV) and establish a flexible multi-model production system.

Hyundai Motor expects the expansion of its India business to translate into more business opportunities for partner companies in a new market. With the completion of the new Pune plant, the number of Korean parts suppliers that have entered India with Hyundai Motor and Kia has reached more than 120. That is 36 more than at the end of 2019, when Kia's Anantapur plant was completed. Partner companies' sales are also rising sharply, with Sungwoo Hitech and Seoyon E-Hwa posting India sales last year of 534.6 billion won and 592.5 billion won, up 54.6% and 97%, respectively, from 2019.

Following the Chennai Plants 1 and 2, Hyundai Motor's third production base in India, the new Pune plant, incorporates smart manufacturing technologies such as an artificial intelligence (AI)-based crack detection system and industrial welding robots. In addition to an automobile assembly plant, it also has an engine plant, a test track, and employee training facilities where Augmented Reality (AR)-based training is conducted.

Hyundai Motor plans to have the new Pune plant handle production of the local strategic model Venue, while pursuing a full electric vehicle (EV) transition at the existing Chennai plant. This aligns with the Indian government's production-linked incentive (PLI—subsidies paid to local EV manufacturers and parts procurement companies) policy under its goal to make 30% of new-vehicle sales electric by 2030.

Considering growing demand in India for electric vehicles and other future mobility, Hyundai Motor plans to launch a new small electric SUV—based on India's vehicle class standards—in the first quarter of next year, adding to the Ioniq 5 and Creta Electric currently on sale. It also plans to train top talent through its technology research center and equip newly launched models with Level 2 Autonomous Driving technology.

It will also invest in startups and new businesses, including collaborating with local two-wheeler maker TVS to develop and commercialize a prototype electric three-wheeler. The amount Hyundai Motor plans to invest by 2032 comes to 20.7 trillion won. To invest efficiently, it is also pushing to establish an investment-specialized corporation in India.

Hyundai Motor Group Chair Chung Eui-sun said at the completion ceremony, "From the first time we entered India 30 years ago, Hyundai Motor worked to earn the trust of local customers. Since launching our first local model, the Santro, India has become a key pillar in Hyundai Motor's global growth," and added, "The completion ceremony of the Pune plant will mark the opening of a new chapter for Hyundai Motor in India."

Attending the ceremony were Chair Chung; Vice Chair Chang Jae-hoon; Hyundai Motor CEO (president) José Muñoz; and Tarun Garg, CEO of Hyundai Motor India Ltd. (HMIL), among other top executives. Also present were Maharashtra Deputy Chief Minister Devendra Fadnavis; Member of Parliament Shrirang Appa Barne; and Lee Seong-ho, Korea's ambassador to India, along with other political and government figures from both countries.

title: 'Not Even Free Money Worked' - The Brutal Truth About Why the Electric Truck Market Collapsed
description:
Here's why... Electric Pickup Sales Are In A Tailspin The numbers look catastrophic at first – but one outlier in this table quietly blows up the standard narrative about why EV sales collapsed.
With the sole exception of the Rivian R1T, every electric pickup has seen a dramatic fall-off into 2026.
EV credits helped to make a lot of new converts, but they haven't been the only factor in electric car adoption.
Exhibit B: incentives that match, or beat, the EV credits have failed to move the needle.
EV credits helped to expand the potential customer base a bit, but the growth was always going to be limited.
text:
In many ways, the end of the tax credits brought the EV segment's momentum to a screeching halt last year. They pulled the $7,500 bonus for qualifying electric vehicles and, seemingly overnight, countless battery-powered cars were discontinued or canceled, and sales plummeted.

We won't argue that there are fewer electric cars on the road today than there would be if those credits were still in place. But, we could argue that electric trucks like the Tesla Cybertruck and the Ford F-150 Lightning would be in essentially the same place they're in right now, with or without the credits. Here's why...

Electric Pickup Sales Are In A Tailspin

The numbers look catastrophic at first – but one outlier in this table quietly blows up the standard narrative about why EV sales collapsed. We're probably not telling you anything you don't know when we say that electric pickup sales have seen brighter days, but let's compare H1 sales for some leading models to see what we're talking about.

With the sole exception of the Rivian R1T, every electric pickup has seen a dramatic fall-off into 2026. Yes, the disappearance of EV credits plays a big part in this decline in sales numbers, but we don't think that's the only reason this has been such a bad year for the segment.

Ford Offered $8,000 Cash Back And Still Couldn't Move The Needle

Exhibit A: Declining sales have been a common, but not uniform, trend in the electric segment. Tesla sold around 1,000 more Model Ys in May and June than it did in the same months in 2025. EV credits helped to make a lot of new converts, but they haven't been the only factor in electric car adoption.

Exhibit B: incentives that match, or beat, the EV credits have failed to move the needle. Ford offered $8,000 cash back incentives on the F-150 Lightning in January this year, and only managed to sell 647 units that month. $8,000 more than makes up for the loss of the $7,500 incentive, and the brand still sold fewer than half as many electric pickups as it had a year prior. Not even free money worked.

These were regional offers, but they were being offered in major metropolitan areas. Additionally, Ford repeated the deal in various regions throughout the rest of H1, and still wound up selling around 16% as many units in H1 as it had in that same stretch of time in 2025.

The Early Adopters Are Gone – And There Aren't Many Buyers Left

We're not arguing that the evaporation of the EV tax credits has not had an impact on electric pickup sales, only that this is not nearly the only factor at play. But what does a market that's truly bottomed out look like? One data point stands out – and it's the one brand that didn't collapse.

The Rivian R1T Sales Numbers Look Better Because They're So Small

Our argument is that, once your early adopters have been taken care of, there aren't that many buyers left. EV credits helped to expand the potential customer base a bit, but the growth was always going to be limited. The Rivian R1T's 2026 sales are actually better than its 2025 sales, which we think helps to support our theory that it's not just the EV credits, and that we're looking at a very small potential market, with or without the credits.

With the sole exception of April, Rivian has been kicking its own butt every single month this year on sales. But, its sales numbers are very small. The R1T hasn't hit four figures in a month since September 2024, when it sold 3,541 units.

We can't tell you exactly what Rivian's sales goals are, or whether these numbers make the brand's investors happy; we can only tell you that 530 sales last June is an easy number to beat. Ford sold 2,200 Lightnings in that same stretch of time last year, an improvement over the year prior, and a number that the brand failed to match in June 2026, at just 491 units sold.

Our hypothesis? A handful of supply-chain hiccups over the years mean that not everyone who wants a Rivian R1T has one just yet. The brand will likely continue selling anywhere from 500 to 600 units a month until those buyers are covered.

While EVs Stall, Hybrid Pickups Are Setting Sales Records Every Month

EVs will likely continue to be a small, niche segment into the coming years, with expensive electric pickups being a niche within that niche. Hybrids, on the other hand, seem to set a new best month, every single month. Earlier this year, Ford sold 33,861 Maverick pickups in Q1, with 17,050 of those being hybrids, accounting for just over half of the total.

The i-Force Max Hybrid Toyota Tacoma only accounted for about 10% of Q1 Tacoma sales, but that comes out to 6,887 units in the first three months of 2026. That's more business than any electric pickup did in that same stretch.

We could go on for pages about why hybrids are more popular than EVs (and we have, more than once), but one key consideration is the fact that you don't need to plan your trips around charging stations.

There's Never Been A Better Time To Buy A Used Electric Pickup

If this all sounds very doom and gloom, the upside is that the auto industry's $1.2 trillion loss is your $42,100 gain. That's what you'll be saving on a 2022 Ford F-150 Lightning Platinum, according to our price tracker tool, which currently sees the top trim trending at just $48,774 from an MSRP of $90,874, representing a 46.3% drop in value after four years on the market.

EVs have been notoriously fast depreciators, thanks in large part to their steep initial costs and the fact that so many of these cars were leased rather than bought, meaning that dealer lots are now flooded with those first-year models. To round up some attractive used listings we were able to find...

A 42,380-mile 2022 Ford F-150 Lightning XLT is selling for $37,990 in Oklahoma.

A 43,692-mile 2023 Ford F-150 Lightning XLT is selling for $40,590 in Nevada.

An 18,072-mile 2023 Ford F-150 Lightning XLT is selling for $49,990 in Texas.

A 12,957-mile 2023 Ford F-150 Lightning XLT is selling for $48,990 in Massachusetts.

A 40,115-mile 2024 Ford F-150 Lightning Flash is selling for $49,990 in Virginia.

These numbers are just to give you an idea of what's out there, but the higher up the trim ladder you go, the more money you'll save, as the depreciation is steepest at the top.

Those who drive electric pickups tend to swear by them. But, Ford spent around $19.5 billion restructuring it's EV plans and getting these cars into production. A small-but-passionate fanbase simply isn't going to cut it at that price.

text:
Los Angeles, October 13, 2026 – Green SM officially launches its all-electric taxi service in Los Angeles, California, marking the company’s first entry into North America and its ninth global market. Green SM brings modern and safe mobility, professionally operated services and good fares to enhance the everyday travel experience for local residents.

Entering Los Angeles brings Green SM into one of the world’s most dynamic and demanding markets. It also marks another step in the international expansion of the Vietnamese mobility brand, following its rapid growth across markets in Asia and Europe.

Starting October 13, customers in Los Angeles can book Green SM rides through the Green SM app, by calling the company’s hotline or by hailing a vehicle on the street. With its growing service network, Green SM will cater to a wide range of mobility needs, from everyday trips and longer journeys to airport transfers.

Green SM is committed to delivering a high-quality customer experience through its 5 Good Promises: Good Cars, Good Drivers, Good Price, Good Experience and Good for the Environment. In Los Angeles, Green SM operates a 100% all-electric fleet of VinFast vehicles, featuring spacious, smooth and modern VinFast VF 8 models; a professional and courteous driver team carefully selected and thoroughly trained; transparent fare information and promotions; and attentive, reliable service designed to give customers rides that are not only greener, but also comfortable and dependable.

To celebrate the launch, new customers who sign up for Green SM will receive 50% off fares, up to USD 12 per ride, on their first five trips. In addition, customers can enjoy a complimentary Green Pass membership, which includes 10 discount vouchers per month, each offering 30% off fares, up to USD 10 per ride.

Ms. Hoang Thanh Hang, CEO of Green SM in the U.S., said: “The United States represents an important milestone in Green SM’s growth journey. We are not simply expanding into a new market. We aim to build trust with customers, drivers and local communities, one journey at a time. Our experience across international markets has shown us that the future of electric mobility is not defined by an all-electric fleet alone. It also depends on service quality, well-trained and reliable drivers, and genuine care in every customer interaction.”

Following the launch, Green SM will gradually build its local team and strengthen its operational capabilities, while recruiting and training local drivers. Through these efforts, Green SM aims not only to create new employment opportunities, but also to make a direct contribution to the transition toward greener mobility in Los Angeles and across the region.

Founded in Vietnam in 2023, Green SM currently operates a green mobility ecosystem across Vietnam, Laos, Indonesia, the Philippines, India, Kazakhstan, Denmark and the Netherlands. As part of its global expansion, Green SM has completed approximately 850 million rides, covering a total distance of nearly 6 billion kilometers, helping reduce more than 800,000 tons of CO₂ emissions, equivalent to the amount of carbon absorbed by approximately 36 million trees.

Green SM’s presence in the United States combines VinFast’s strengths in all-electric vehicles with Green SM’s operational expertise, giving customers an additional option for smooth, comfortable and zero-emission mobility. This also marks an important milestone in the global growth journey of the Vietnamese all-electric ride-hailing company. From Los Angeles, Green SM will continue investing in its fleet, technology, driver team and service quality, putting customer experience at the heart of its sustainable growth in the U.S. and international markets./.

title: What a time to take the wheel - Auto retail faces disruption, but opportunity remains firmly ahead
authors: Lucas Malinowski, Ian Cruickshank, Duane Marino, Wolfgang Koehler, Blair Qualey, Canadian Auto Dealer, Perry Lefko
description:
The automotive industry has always been at the forefront of innovation and industrial imagination.
Cars are safer, faster, more reliable, luxurious and technologically advanced than ever before, all while maintaining affordability relative to inflation.
Looking across the river at GM’s Renaissance Centre and visiting my first North American International Auto Show in Detroit ensured that initial obsession would always be in the back of my mind, no matter what I ended up doing in life.
Another obsession with history and politics took me down a professional path of working in government, communications and public affairs.
The automotive industry has always been at the forefront of innovation and industrial imagination.
text:
One of my earliest childhood memories is walking through Nuremberg with my parents and my father challenging me to name the marque of every passing car on the busy streets.

Our family had recently escaped communist Poland, where the drab selection of Soviet-approved personal transportation didn’t quite spark the imagination of this fledgling car enthusiast in the same way the shiny and bright offerings of West Germany did toward the end of the Cold War.

I was hooked, and have always taken pride in being able to identify even the most obscure OEM badges and models wherever my travels took me.

Windsor was where my family initially called home in Canada, and for the first time in my life I actually met people who worked in the auto industry. For a living!

The automotive industry has always been at the forefront of innovation and industrial imagination. Cars are safer, faster, more reliable, luxurious and technologically advanced than ever before, all while maintaining affordability relative to inflation.

Looking across the river at GM’s Renaissance Centre and visiting my first North American International Auto Show in Detroit ensured that initial obsession would always be in the back of my mind, no matter what I ended up doing in life.

Another obsession with history and politics took me down a professional path of working in government, communications and public affairs. But the passion for all things automotive was always there, albeit in a personal rather than professional capacity.

That all changed in 2023 when I jumped at the chance to merge the two things that keep me up at night and join the team at Global Automakers of Canada. The past three years have provided a unique opportunity to grow from being passionate about cars to understanding the automotive industry, which for more than a century has sparked imaginations and obsessions around the world.

Now, the members of Global Automakers have given me the privilege and responsibility of representing the interests of an industry in the midst of truly profound change.

The automotive industry has always been at the forefront of innovation and industrial imagination. Cars are safer, faster, more reliable, luxurious and technologically advanced than ever before, all while maintaining affordability relative to inflation.

We have a history of meeting and exceeding challenges initially thought insurmountable, and have grown into a globally integrated industry where innovation knows few borders. But many of the underpinnings of the past century’s success are being stressed in new and multiple ways at once, particularly in Canada.

Automotive tariffs and a rupture in the highly integrated North American market are adding significant costs across the supply chain and impacting the competitiveness of the region’s manufacturing base. We need to get back to tariff-free auto trade to keep North America competitive for the dozens of Global Automakers who build cars in the region.

The transition to electrification requires new product development and production methods, along with significant capital investments from automakers.

It also requires outside players, such as charging providers, to do their part to support consumer demand, along with new consumer education.

EVs are getting better every day, but a significant percentage of drivers remain concerned that they’re not the right fit for their needs, particularly in North America.

A significant turn away from electrification in the United States could create a situation down the road where North American drivers don’t have access to the latest and greatest vehicle technologies deployed around the world — an unimaginable thought for a younger me calling out every single nameplate my father pointed at.

Either of these developments on their own would represent a generational shift in the history of the industry. But we also have to add the incredibly rapid rise of Chinese automotive manufacturing and significant export capacity that is making its impact on markets around the globe.

Automakers are competitors by nature and have always compared their own products against segment leaders to find ways they can improve the next generation. But there are serious and real questions about how competing with Chinese OEMs can be done on a level playing field.

As it looks to open our market to these new entrants, the Government of Canada will face a significant challenge in balancing fair competition that supports the benefits of our own domestic manufacturing with the need to address affordability for drivers.

I must admit that on a recent family vacation to a Central American country with significant Chinese imports, for the first time in my life I found myself passing cars with nameplates I’d never seen or heard of before. While humbling, it was also exciting to be reminded that there’s always something new to learn about automotive.

This is a daunting time for our industry, but we have shown over and over again our ability to adapt and thrive despite the roadblocks ahead. And as we all know, it’s the twisty roads that make for the best driving.

text:
Swedish transport company Einride was an early pioneer in the development of autonomous electric trucks—the company has a cabless autonomous truck that has been running in pilots for several years. However, the company hasn’t put all its electric eggs in the autonomous basket—it operates a large heavy-duty EV charging site in California, and in August it placed an order for 500 Tesla Semis.

Now autonomous trucking is starting to happen. Einride has two of its cabless, driverless electric trucks running scheduled routes with EASE Logistics in Marysville, Ohio. The operations are part of the Truck Automation Corridor Project, a joint effort of the Ohio Department of Transportation (ODOT), DriveOhio, and the Indiana Department of Transportation. This is EASE’s third autonomous trucking deployment with DriveOhio.

“EASE believes in leading through action and putting innovation to work in real-world operations,” said Peter Coratola Jr, President and CEO of EASE Logistics. “This deployment builds on that commitment while helping advance the adoption of autonomous freight across the transportation industry.”

Einride’s vehicles are capable of SAE Level 4-autonomous mode, meaning that they operate without a human in the cab—a remote operator monitors each truck off-site and can intervene if needed. The trucks run on local public roads, carrying freight between EASE facilities. The deployment is generating operational data on safety, reliability and efficiency that will inform how autonomous freight scales beyond this initial route.

“This deployment reflects the maturity of our purpose-built autonomous stack, combining driverless operation with remote oversight to run safely in real-world operations,” said Henrik Green, CTO at Einride. “Daily operations in Marysville give us the proof points we need to keep expanding autonomous freight across the corridor and beyond.”

title: Per-Vehicle Cost 73,000 Yuan Higher Than China: Europe Cannot Block Chinese Cars ... - 36氪
description:
Data from the US firm AlixPartners shows that Chinese automakers can produce an electric vehicle at a cost of $20,000, while similar competing models in Europe cost $31,000, a difference of $11,000, equivalent to 73,000 RMB.
Even with taxation, Chinese electric vehicles still retain huge cost advantages.
Quotas and additional tariffs cannot stop Chinese vehicles Tariffs and quotas have not stopped the pace of Chinese automobiles.
In addition, in the past two years, local European automakers such as Volkswagen and BBA have accelerated their new energy transformation.
Tariffs and quotas are emergency measures for Europe to protect its local industries, and Chinese automakers choose to respond with system-based overseas expansion.
text:
The numerous recent news stories emerging between China and Europe are sparks generated by another head-on collision between two automotive industry systems.

The price gap between vehicle models at home and abroad is vaguely perceived by the market. Everyone knows that Chinese cars are cheaper than foreign ones, but consumers do not have a clear idea of how much lower the price is exactly.

Recently, a commercial consulting firm has given the answer to this question.

Data from the US firm AlixPartners shows that Chinese automakers can produce an electric vehicle at a cost of $20,000, while similar competing models in Europe cost $31,000, a difference of $11,000, equivalent to 73,000 RMB.

This is the manufacturing-side cost. The terminal selling price is also affected by factors such as brand, positioning, market, and tariffs. Especially overseas, tariffs can even double the selling price compared to the domestic market.

European politicians hope to close this $11,000 gap with tariffs, but analysts point out that tariffs cannot eliminate the structural cost gap, and can only weaken price competitiveness. Even with taxation, Chinese electric vehicles still retain huge cost advantages. Because this advantage does not come from government subsidies, but is jointly determined by the supply chain cluster, independent R&D of enterprises and economies of scale.

Surge in sales of independent brands, Europe is getting more and more nervous

Driven by the overseas expansion strategy, Chinese independent brands such as Geely, SAIC, BYD, and Chery have continued to make efforts in the European market, with a growth performance that is so outstanding that it catches the eye.

According to Dataforce statistics, from January to August this year, the cumulative sales of Chinese passenger vehicles in the European market reached 913,000 units, a year-on-year increase of 111%, 24 times the growth rate of the overall market; the corresponding market share increased from 5.2% in the same period last year to 9.9%. Looking at August alone, the market share of Chinese brand passenger vehicles further climbed to 11.7%.

The local electrification process in Europe has also accelerated, with the penetration rate of electric vehicles reaching 29% in August, and the average penetration rate from January to August being 23%. There is no doubt that new energy has become the core engine of growth in the European automotive market, and Chinese brands are an important source of incremental growth in this sector.

In the first three quarters of this year, the total sales of electric vehicles in 14 core European countries reached 1.867 million units, a year-on-year increase of 36.15%; among them, the sales of Chinese brand electric vehicles reached 371,300 units, a sharp year-on-year increase of 79.12%, significantly higher than the overall market growth rate.

Looking at the TOP20 list of electric vehicle sales in Europe, the listed Chinese enterprises include BYD, Leapmotor, MG, XPeng, and Geely. Excluding the extreme year-on-year increase of 21296.97% caused by Geely's extremely low base, Leapmotor's sales growth exceeded 5 times, XPeng's growth reached 167%; BYD ranked seventh, and still maintained a growth rate of more than 70% on the premise of a large existing sales base.

It is worth noting that this round of growth occurred after the European Union imposed a maximum 45.3% tariff on Chinese pure electric models in 2024.

The implementation of tariffs did not block the export growth of Chinese automakers, but only the export structure has changed slightly: the growth rate of pure electric models has slowed down, and the export of plug-in hybrid models has accelerated more rapidly.

Eurostat data shows that the EU imported 107,000 hybrid vehicles from China in 2024, and the figure rose to 302,000 in 2025; as for this year, in July alone, the EU imported 50,400 Chinese plug-in hybrid vehicles, a sharp year-on-year increase of 163.2%.

The rapid rise in plug-in hybrid imports has also become the direct trigger for the EU to recently brew restrictions on the trade of Chinese plug-in hybrid vehicles. Earlier, the EU proposed an agreement requiring China to cut its exports of hybrid vehicles to Europe by more than half within four years, amounting to one million units.

Bloomberg reported that the quota is based on 2025 trade data, allowing 350,000 Chinese hybrid vehicles to be imported in the first year, and the quota will increase by 6% every year from the second year; the policy cycle lasts for four years. Calculated in this way, the total four-year quota is about 1.5 million units.

According to data from the Financial Times, if the growth rate in July is maintained, the total import volume in 2026 will reach 600,000 units, 70% higher than the first-year quota in the report, which shows that there is a clear mismatch between the original quota scheme and the real growth rhythm of the market.

There is no specific quota information in China's response. On the 12th, the Ministry of Commerce stated that China and Europe have reached a consensus on the trade of hybrid and electric vehicles, setting up an incremental arrangement based on the 2025 level to ensure the export space and stable growth of Chinese enterprises, and take into account the actual demands and reasonable concerns of the industries of both sides.

Although trade frictions continue to heat up, and tariff and quota tools have appeared one after another, market data shows that such policy measures have not curbed the expansion momentum of Chinese automobiles in Europe. Trade restrictions can only adjust the export structure, and it is difficult to shake the deep-seated competitive foundation behind it.

Quotas and additional tariffs cannot stop Chinese vehicles

Tariffs and quotas have not stopped the pace of Chinese automobiles.

The rapid expansion of Chinese automakers in the European market is supported by both product power and price.

In terms of product power, Chinese new energy vehicles have indeed established differentiated advantages by virtue of intelligence and electrification in the past.

However, European consumers' demand for intelligence is significantly lower than that of domestic consumers. In addition, in the past two years, local European automakers such as Volkswagen and BBA have accelerated their new energy transformation. Products such as Mercedes-Benz pure electric CLA, GLC, and BMW new generation iX3 have received good responses in the regional market, and the product power of local brands is catching up rapidly.

In contrast, price is still the core competitiveness of Chinese brands. As mentioned earlier, independent brand electric vehicles have a $11,000 manufacturing-side cost advantage over European competing products, and in the terminal sales scenario, the price gap of the same model between China and Europe is further widened.

The average domestic price of NIO Firefly is 126,500 RMB, and the average price in Thailand is 161,000 RMB; in Europe, Norway has the lowest selling price at about 180,000 RMB, and Hungary has the highest average price at 262,000 RMB, which is directly double the average domestic price. The average domestic price of XPeng L03 is 140,300 RMB, Norway is also the market with the lowest average price for XPeng in Europe, at about 257,700 RMB, an increase of 83% over the domestic price; Switzerland has the highest average price, reaching 333,400 RMB.

From A0-class small cars under 100,000 RMB to high-end flagship models above 500,000 RMB, there is generally a significant average price gap between models in the domestic and European markets, which is far higher than the 45.3% tariff barrier. Even with cross-border logistics costs added, Chinese models still maintain considerable competitiveness compared with local European products.

A typical example is Denza Z9 GT, whose domestic guide price is less than 400,000 RMB, and the European market is priced at 115,000 euros, directly targeting the Porsche Taycan.

The huge price gap has also made European policy makers misjudge the competition logic of Chinese automakers, which has led to trade intervention measures in the name of "fair competition".

As for the EU quota, the German Association of the Automotive Industry (VDA) evaluates the policy based on whether it contributes to fair competition, creates planning certainty, and strengthens open and rule-based trade. The focus also falls on fairness.

However, protection measures such as tariffs and quotas can only treat the symptoms in the short term, and cannot reverse the pattern fundamentally, because the cost advantage of Chinese automakers is rooted in faster R&D iteration speed, independent software architecture and full-chain supply chain management capabilities.

In terms of R&D cycle, Chinese automakers generally only need 24 months to develop a new model, while similar projects of European automakers often take as long as 60 months; 76%-100% of the sales of Chinese automakers come from new models launched in the past three years, while the proportion of European automakers is only 33%.

In terms of supply chain, the layout of the European supply chain is relatively scattered, and automakers' parts mainly rely on imports. The long-distance transportation of parts pushes up time and capital costs.

On the one hand, Chinese automakers have begun to deploy large-scale independent R&D and production of core components such as batteries, chips, and motors. Data from the International Energy Agency shows that the price of Chinese cells is more than 30% lower than that in Europe; on the other hand, the domestic automotive supply chain cluster continues to iterate, with prominent industrial agglomeration effects, accounting for more than 80% of the global power battery manufacturing and raw material production capacity, and contributing more than half of the global electric vehicle output. Relying on the huge market size, the manufacturing cost per vehicle can be continuously diluted.

Even if additional expenses such as tariffs and cross-border logistics need to be borne for sales to Europe, automakers can still rely on the underlying manufacturing cost advantage, combined with higher overseas terminal selling prices, to hedge the additional cost pressure brought by overseas expansion.

Next stop: system-based overseas expansion

Although tariff barriers can hardly stop the expansion of Chinese automakers, with a large number of independent brands pouring into the European market, the industry needs to cope with more diverse and complex long-term challenges.

The Paris Motor Show has become an important window to observe the European strategies of Chinese automakers. At this Paris Motor Show, 16 Chinese automakers with 25 brands participated in the exhibition, and their booth area accounted for one third of the entire exhibition, exceeding the sum of the participating brands from France and Germany.

However, the attitude of the European industrial sector is not friendly. On the eve of the Paris Motor Show, French President Emmanuel Macron held a closed-door dinner at the Élysée Palace, where vehicle groups, parts giants, battery and rare earth tycoons gathered, but there were no familiar faces for Chinese consumers. The abrupt statement that "Chinese exhibitors will not participate in this dinner" shut Chinese exhibitors out.

Nevertheless, the rejected Chinese automakers have not slowed down their pace. In this ambiguous atmosphere, the Chinese brands participating in this exhibition no longer simply aim to release new cars, but focus on disclosing their European localized implementation strategies. System-based overseas expansion has become a consensus.

Among new power brands, XPeng is promoting localized production in Europe, and G9L has been put into production at the Magna factory in Austria and opened for European reservations; Leapmotor relies on Stellantis' mature channels to expand the market, will continue to iterate products and deepen localized operations.

Li Auto, which participated in the exhibition for the first time, brought the i6 and also brought Li Auto's restrained European strategy of "small market verification and then replication". In the first quarter of next year, the i6 will be launched in Europe, first entering small markets with high pure electric penetration rates such as Norway and the Netherlands to verify brand capabilities. Li Auto will follow the restrained strategy of "small market verification and then replication" in Europe, and after running through the service closed loop, it will expand to core markets such as Germany, France and the United Kingdom.

Geely Auto Group gathered in Paris with three major brands: Geely, Lynk & Co, and Zeekr. Geely has laid out in Europe for nearly 20 years, and will take Europe as the base of its globalization capabilities in the future, and export R&D, product, channel and manufacturing capabilities together. Recently, Geely has reached a cooperation with Ford in Europe, and the two sides will jointly build a joint venture company and share production capacity.

GAC has also entered a new stage of full-link localized deep cultivation in Europe, accelerating its layout in R&D, production, market and energy.

It is not difficult to see that the consensus of independent brands in Europe in the next stage is "system-based overseas expansion": to open up the complete chain of R&D, production, sales and after-sales, and export system capabilities at the same time.

Although the direction of overseas expansion is clear, automakers still face dual internal and external pressures.

At the domestic level, starting from April next year, the export tax rebate rate for value-added tax on new energy vehicles will be reduced from 13% to 9%. According to calculations, for every 100,000 RMB of ex-factory price excluding tax, the export cost will increase by 4,000 RMB.

The policy adjustment will weaken the cost advantage of pure electric vehicles going overseas at low prices, but it is beneficial to fuel and HEV products, which may in the short term prompt automakers to stock up overseas in advance before the spring of next year. In the long run, this change will force new energy automakers to break away from simple price competition, accelerate overseas localized implementation, and turn to rely on product power and brand value to participate in market competition.

On the overseas side, a large number of Chinese brands are entering the market intensively, and the competition on the European track continues to intensify. The growth mode that simply relies on low prices is unsustainable. At the same time, if automakers build factories in Europe, local production will gradually weaken the original cost advantage of domestic manufacturing.

From price difference to tariffs, from tariffs to quotas, Europe's defense tools against Chinese automobiles are constantly upgrading, but the offensive means of Chinese automakers are also becoming more diverse.

The numerous recent news stories emerging between China and Europe are sparks generated by another head-on collision between two automotive industry systems. Tariffs and quotas are emergency measures for Europe to protect its local industries, and Chinese automakers choose to respond with system-based overseas expansion.

text:
EM leader joined federal, state and industry leaders at South Carolina Nuclear Summit to discuss new nuclear and super intelligence missions on DOE land

COLUMBIA, S.C. — Assistant Secretary for Environmental Management (EM) Tim Walsh recently joined more than 600 leaders at the third annual South Carolina Nuclear Summit to discuss how U.S. Department of Energy (DOE) land is becoming a springboard for America's nuclear renaissance.

Walsh delivered remarks following Gov. Henry McMaster, then joined a panel focused on how federal land is becoming the platform for advanced nuclear and super intelligence infrastructure.

Walsh said EM's 15 remaining legacy sites helped the nation win World War II and the Cold War and are being revitalized to help America lead the world in energy production, advanced manufacturing and super intelligence (SI).

"The faster we can get things cleaned up, the faster we can turn that land over to more productive use," said Walsh.

Moderated by Robbie Bennett, president and CEO of the SRS Community Reuse Organization, the panel included leaders from the companies Amentum, DC BLOX, Antares Nuclear, Oklo Inc. and Newcleo.

The Savannah River Site (SRS), about an hour from the summit venue, offers a model for the transition to advanced nuclear and SI. Walsh highlighted H Canyon, the nation's only production-scale chemical separations facility, which EM is using to turn used nuclear fuel once slated for disposal into high-assay low-enriched uranium. He also pointed to the decision to restart HB-Line, which EM expects to accelerate its plutonium disposition mission by 10 to 13 years and save taxpayers up to $350 million.

Walsh also called for rebuilding the workforce needed to construct nuclear plants at scale and praised South Carolina, including the University of South Carolina, for taking a leadership role.

Associate Deputy Secretary of Energy Alex Fitzsimmons and Julie Kozeracki of DOE's Office of Energy Dominance Financing also spoke at the summit.

"There is no better place in my mind to bring it all together than right here in South Carolina to ensure our nuclear renaissance actually happens," Walsh said. "My motto is GSD — get stuff done — and we're going to get started here in South Carolina."

Revolution Wind received its federal and state permits after a more than nine-year-long process spanning multiple agencies.

text:
After halting construction on offshore wind farms and canceling leases for future projects, the Trump administration just took another step to erode America’s troubled offshore wind industry.

The Interior Department wants to reevaluate a key approval for Revolution Wind — a $6.2 billion project that is already producing power off the coasts of Connecticut and Rhode Island. The wind farm began generating electricity in March, and its developer Ørsted installed the last of 65 turbines in September.

On Friday, Interior asked a federal court for permission to remand the agency’s 2023 approval of a construction and operations plan for the 704-megawatt wind farm. Experts say the move doesn’t immediately affect the project’s activities and is part of a longer legal process that could drag on into early next year.

Even so, the new filing ​“injects uncertainty into a nearly completed offshore wind project that electricity planners and consumers in the Northeast are counting on,” Hillary Bright, executive director of the offshore wind advocacy group Turn Forward, said in an emailed statement.

At full operation, Revolution Wind will generate enough clean electricity to power over 350,000 homes and is expected to play an important role in reducing the region’s grid stress during heat waves and winter cold spells.

The Trump administration’s Oct. 9 filing stems from an ongoing lawsuit filed by the anti-wind group Green Oceans, which bills itself as a grassroots organization dedicated to preserving ocean health. In January 2024, the Rhode Island-based group challenged Interior’s final approvals of both Revolution Wind and Ørsted’s other U.S. offshore wind project, South Fork Wind, which came online in early 2024.

Green Oceans claims that the federal government ​“shortcut” regulatory procedures and violated environmental protection laws by approving the two projects. Late last week, Interior essentially said that it agrees that the key permits should be remanded and asked a judge to close the case against the agency. Revolution Wind received its federal and state permits after a more than nine-year-long process spanning multiple agencies.

The judge overseeing the request is Judge Royce Lamberth of the U.S. District Court for the District of Columbia, who has previously sided with offshore wind developers that were forced to pause construction last year under the Trump administration’s stop-work orders.

“From its very first day, the Trump administration has waged a war on clean energy, and especially offshore wind,” said Pasha Feinberg, an offshore wind strategist at the Natural Resources Defense Council.

She said that, as utility bills soar and electricity demand climbs across the region, Revolution Wind is helping to keep electricity bills in check for residents of Connecticut and Rhode Island. ​“Why the administration would even consider revoking its permit makes no sense,” she added.

text:
Company marks occasion with anniversary webpage highlighting projects over the years

NEW ORLEANS, LA / ACCESS Newswire / October 13, 2026 / By Cole Avery

Entergy is commemorating the 25th anniversary of its Environmental Initiatives Fund, marking a milestone in a long history of environmental commitment that began well before sustainability became a corporate trend.

For a quarter century, Entergy's EIF has exemplified the company's early and ongoing leadership in environmental stewardship. Established in 2001 as a shareholder-funded grant program, the EIF represents a proactive approach to protecting natural resources, reducing emissions, restoring habitats and strengthening community resilience across Arkansas, Louisiana, Mississippi and Texas. Over its 25-year history, Entergy shareholders have invested nearly $45 million in community-based environmental improvements across the region.

"Reaching 25 years of the Environmental Initiatives Fund is more than marking time; it's a reaffirmation of a commitment our shareholders embraced long before sustainability was in the spotlight," said John Weiss, vice president of sustainability and environmental policy. "The EIF has allowed us to support meaningful projects that improve local ecosystems, strengthen communities and advance environmental progress throughout our service area."

In 2025 alone, the EIF provided $1 million in shareholder-funded support to 11 partner organizations working in areas such as wetland restoration, tree planting, biodiversity education and green infrastructure development. These efforts complement Entergy's broader environmental initiatives, including long-term climate commitments, coastal restoration partnerships and decades of community-focused conservation work.

This anniversary highlights a broader legacy in climate action for Entergy. In 2001 - the same year the EIF launched - Entergy became the first U.S. utility to voluntarily limit its carbon emissions, signaling a level of environmental responsibility uncommon at the time. Two decades later, Entergy operates one of the cleanest large-scale power generation fleets in the United States and is a nationally recognized leader in sustainability, reinforcing the company's long-term commitment to climate action, environmental reporting and performance across key sustainability indicators.

Anniversary webpage highlights progress, partnerships

To mark the 25-year milestone, Entergy has introduced a commemorative webpage featuring:

A video message from Entergy sustainability leadership

An interactive map showcasing highlighted projects across the service area

Profiles of partner organizations across the service region

Learn more about the Environmental Initiatives Fund's 25-year impact and explore the anniversary content at Entergy.com/Environment/EIF.

We're focused on keeping costs for our customers as low as possible while providing reliable energy that our communities count on. We're also investing in growth for the future with a more resilient, cleaner energy system that includes modern natural gas, nuclear and renewable energy generation. As a nationally recognized leader in sustainability and corporate citizenship, we deliver more than $100 million in economic benefits each year to the communities we serve through philanthropy, volunteerism and advocacy. text:
“We can’t build Ohio’s energy future if it takes up to a decade just to get a permit.”

COLUMBUS – Sen. Jon Husted (R-Ohio) today hosted a permitting reform roundtable with Senate Majority Whip John Barrasso (R-Wyo.), bringing together state lawmakers, regulators and Ohio energy, manufacturing and business leaders.

Currently, a federal environmental review can take up to a decade. Projects miss deadlines and waste budgets before construction begins. As energy usage adds demand to Ohio’s grid, the grid must keep up.

“Ohio’s economy is growing, and the grid has to keep up. We can’t build Ohio’s energy future and lower costs for working families if it takes up to a decade just to get a permit. I was glad to bring my friend Sen. Barrasso to Columbus to hear directly from the people who build, power and regulate energy in Ohio. We’re also fighting to make sure data centers pay for their own energy so working families aren’t stuck footing the bill for Big Tech,” said Husted.

“America needs to build better, faster, cheaper, and smarter. Right now, critical energy projects spend years trapped in the regulatory penalty box. Senator Husted’s roundtable today underscored how essential permitting reform is to producing more American energy and lowering prices for American families. Senator Husted has led the way in the Senate with thoughtful legislation that will protect families from increased electricity rates. The Senate has also negotiated bipartisan permitting legislation. We need to pass these reforms this year. American families cannot afford to wait,” said Barrasso.

Husted is a member of the Senate Environment and Public Works Committee and has worked with Chairman Shelley Moore Capito (R-W.Va.) on fixing our broken permitting system. He also introduced the Ratepayer Protection Act, which would make large new data centers pay for their own energy costs, and worked to include stronger protections in the permitting bill.

Husted is also leading efforts in the Senate on permitting reform including:

The New Source Review Permitting Act, which would clarify federal permitting requirements under the Clean Air Act to help manufacturers and energy producers improve efficiency, upgrade equipment and complete pollution control projects.

The American Energy and Mineral Infrastructure Act of 2026, which would streamline federal permitting, reduce delays from litigation and overlapping reviews, and accelerate construction of critical energy and mineral infrastructure.

The Water Authority and Timely Environmental Review (WATER Act), which aims to streamline permitting for water projects.

Participants discussed the Bipartisan American Affordability and Jobs Act, a U.S. Senate bill that would make the permitting process more efficient, effective and predictable while keeping environmental safeguards intact and protecting. The bill is expected to receive a vote in the U.S. Senate when senators return to the Capitol after the October state work period. They also discussed ways to add grid capacity by upgrading existing power lines.

Federal law requires projects like power plants, pipelines and roads to undergo lengthy reviews before construction starts. Those reviews are often open-ended, and permits can be challenged in court for years. The Bipartisan American Affordability and Jobs Act would:

Set deadlines. Environmental assessments would be due within one year and full environmental impact statements within two years.

Limit lawsuits. Claims under the National Environmental Policy Act would have to be filed within 150 days.

Protect issued permits. Federal agencies couldn’t pull or suspend a valid permit except under specific conditions.

Protect ratepayers, using a similar solution to Husted’s Ratepayer Protection Act. Data centers using 20 megawatts or more would have to cover their own energy costs.

Keep Ohio in control. Ohio keeps its authority to site transmission lines and sets rates for data centers.

title: IRENA Projects Fossil Fuel, Conventional Energy Share Of Jobs To Fall To 16% By 2050
description:
Global energy sector employment could reach 343.1 million jobs by 2050 under the Decarbonising Energy Scenario (DES), more than three times the 103.2 million jobs recorded in 2024, according to the International Renewable Energy Agency (IRENA).
In 2024, fossil fuels and conventional technologies accounted for approximately 63.4 million jobs, or just over 60% of total energy sector employment.
This category would become the largest contributor to energy sector employment, accounting for approximately 35% of total jobs under the scenario.
Developing Economies To Account For Over 70% Of Energy Sector Jobs Under the DES, global energy sector employment is projected to be heavily concentrated in developing regions by 2050.
Together, these regions and countries would represent more than 70% of global energy sector employment.
text:
Global energy sector employment could reach 343.1 million jobs by 2050 under the Decarbonising Energy Scenario (DES), more than three times the 103.2 million jobs recorded in 2024, according to the International Renewable Energy Agency (IRENA).

The most significant change under the DES is expected to be structural. In 2024, fossil fuels and conventional technologies accounted for approximately 63.4 million jobs, or just over 60% of total energy sector employment. By 2050, their share is projected to decline to around 16% under the DES.

Under the Planned Energy Scenario (PES), however, employment in this category is projected to remain considerably higher, at 108.5 million jobs. In contrast, employment in other transition-related technologies is projected to increase sharply from 7.4 million jobs in 2024 to 121.2 million by 2050 under the DES. This category would become the largest contributor to energy sector employment, accounting for approximately 35% of total jobs under the scenario.

The shift indicates a transition from a workforce dominated by fossil fuels and conventional technologies towards employment opportunities across a broader range of technologies supporting the energy transition.

Energy Transition To Reshape Global Employment Structure

The DES envisages a transformation in the composition and geographical distribution of the global energy workforce, supported by increased investment in clean technologies, energy efficiency and supporting infrastructure.

Under the PES, global energy sector employment is projected to reach 268.7 million jobs by 2050, more than 70 million fewer than under the DES. The difference is already evident by 2030, when employment is projected to reach 239.6 million jobs under the DES, compared with 178.2 million under the PES.

Although employment is projected to grow under both scenarios, the DES is expected to support a larger and more diversified workforce across different time horizons and value-chain segments. The projections highlight the potential for decarbonisation to drive employment growth alongside the transformation of energy systems.

Developing Economies To Account For Over 70% Of Energy Sector Jobs

Under the DES, global energy sector employment is projected to be heavily concentrated in developing regions by 2050. Sub-Saharan Africa is expected to account for the largest share, at 32.5%, followed by East Asia at 21.9%, with China accounting for the dominant share of employment in the latter region. India is projected to account for 18.5%. Together, these regions and countries would represent more than 70% of global energy sector employment.

The IRENA report identifies a significant geographical shift in the relative distribution of employment between East Asia and Sub-Saharan Africa by 2050. Several demographic and economic factors underpin this change. Over the coming decades, China's population is expected to decline even as its gross domestic product (GDP) grows, while Africa's population is projected to increase substantially, particularly among younger age groups.

Employment intensities in Africa are also significantly higher than in China and East Asia. Consequently, investment demand is more likely to translate into increased employment in Africa, where the capital stock starts from a substantially lower base and takes time to generate higher productivity.

The remaining energy sector jobs are projected to be distributed across other regions. The Middle East and North Africa (MENA) and the 'Rest of World' are each expected to account for approximately 6% of employment. Latin America is projected to hold a 5.2% share, followed by Europe at 4.3%, Southeast Asia at 3%, North America at 2.2% and Oceania at 0.3%.

These projections underscore the growing importance of Africa and Asia in the global energy workforce, reflecting demographic trends, rising energy demand and the employment potential of energy-transition investments. Europe and North America, by comparison, are projected to account for a combined 6.5% of global energy sector employment.

Solar To Lead Renewable Energy Employment Growth

Solar energy is projected to become the largest employer within the renewable energy sector, with employment increasing from approximately 7.9 million jobs in 2024 to 38.3 million by 2050 under the DES.

Solar would account for nearly half of all renewable energy employment and support 11.7 million more jobs than under the PES in 2050.

Bioenergy is expected to be the second-largest contributor to renewable energy employment, with approximately 29.5 million jobs projected under the DES by 2050.

Wind energy employment is also expected to expand substantially, increasing more than fivefold from over 1.9 million jobs in 2024 to approximately 11.1 million by 2050 under the DES. This represents 4.9 million more jobs than projected under the PES. The growth is expected to be supported by the expansion of onshore wind and accelerating offshore wind deployment.

Hydropower employment is projected to grow more modestly, reaching approximately 4.5 million jobs by 2050. This reflects the maturity of the technology and the declining availability of greenfield project sites.

Geothermal energy and other renewable technologies are expected to remain relatively small employers in absolute terms, although they are projected to record rapid percentage growth. These technologies could create niche employment opportunities, particularly in regions with favourable resource endowments.

text:
For a second year, Butler’s Office of Sustainability is hosting its ‘Sustainability at the Roots’ speaker series. The event aims to teach students how they can lead and advocate for a sustainable lifestyle.

The theme of this year’s series is how the environment can impact people through their surroundings, such as the air, water and soil. Spread across four events throughout October and into early November, each session will tackle a different environmental aspect.

The speakers for these sessions hail from multiple local environmental agencies, including the Indiana Department of Environmental Management (IDEM), Indianapolis Office of Sustainability, The White River Alliance, Indiana Brownfields Program and the Marion County Public Health Department.

On Oct. 9, the first lecture of the four-part series took place — welcoming IDEM’s senior environmental manager Emma Foust and environmental manager Anna Meyers, as well as Lindsay Trameri, a project manager at the Indianapolis Office of Sustainability, to speak on air pollution in Indiana.

Throughout their presentations, they explained to students how air pollution is primarily caused, the science behind it, how it is measured and what is being done to combat it, both in Indianapolis and statewide. Students also learned about ways they can get involved and stay informed through resources such as Knozone and SmogWatch.

Meyers hopes the event showed students that there are dedicated people working diligently every day to keep Indiana’s air clean.

“I [hope] people [learned] more about the different roles and jobs that are out there pertaining to air quality,” Meyers said. “There are people [working behind the scenes] who care and are looking out for the environment.”

Another main point of the series is examining the crossroads between sustainability, job choice and advocacy. Trameri is optimistic that these presentations showed the connections between the three subjects.

“It seemed like everyone who came had a different major, which is great,” Trameri said. “I hope they left understanding a bit more about the intersection of air quality and their chosen course of study and goal career path, and how we’re really talking about public health when we’re talking about air quality and [how that] overlaps with everything any of us does in our careers and in our lives.”

MaCie’ Weathers, the associate director of sustainability education and outreach, says it can be scary to hear how big a role the environment plays in human health; however, these lectures are designed to get students on that topic. Their goal is not to fearmonger, but to start some uneasy conversations that will help students navigate the world of sustainability.

“[There are] a lot of things we don’t have control over [regarding the environment],” Weathers said. “It’s a part of us to be cognizant, learn more [and] have more education around these areas, because whether we want to accept it or not, things outside of our control are impacting us, and it’s important to know what you can do as an individual, as a citizen [and] as an active member in the community. You can decide to be a person every day who makes real choices that impact not only you but the communities around you.”

title: A 250-kilowatt induction furnace in Utah's coal country is set to get heat pipes so it can fake ...
description:
And it’s lined up for a pretty strange new job, pretending to be the inside of a nuclear reactor.
The company says the furnace will get heat pipes, sensors, and some purpose-built parts.
Many laptops use thin copper heat pipes to draw heat away from the processor.
The company describes NuSun as a solid-state, heat-pipe-cooled reactor, meaning the heat pipes are the cooling system.
Westinghouse built its eVinci microreactor around heat pipes too, and a scaled-down eVinci core went critical in Nevada this summer.
text:
Ever cooked on an induction stove? Basically, they use a magnetic field to make the pan heat itself up, which is why the surface doesn’t glow red like the coil on an old electric stove.

Now, expand that process. The Utah San Rafael Energy Lab (USREL), a state-run research site in Emery County, has a much bigger version of that trick: a 250-kilowatt induction furnace. And it’s lined up for a pretty strange new job, pretending to be the inside of a nuclear reactor.

NuCube Energy, a microreactor startup based in Idaho Falls, said on October 6 that it’s moving on to its next round of USREL testing, with researchers from Brigham Young University along for the ride. The company says the furnace will get heat pipes, sensors, and some purpose-built parts. Engineers will then be able to dial the furnace’s heat up and down to match what NuSun, the startup’s reactor design, is meant to produce.

There’s no start date in the announcement, so don’t expect results next week. Or months, knowing how these things go.

So why fake a reactor at all?

Because real nuclear fuel comes with a lot of strings attached. You need federal sign-off to load it, security to guard it, and a supplier willing to sell it to you, and none of that happens quickly. Once a core has actually run, it’s radioactive too, so if a sensor dies or a weld cracks, you can’t exactly pop the lid off and take a look. Electric heat lets engineers break things, fix them and break them again for the price of a power bill. It’s the sensible order in which to do things.

It isn’t a new idea, however. Over in Italy, a full-size, lead-cooled reactor stand-in is built around banks of electric heaters sitting where its fuel would go.

So what’s a heat pipe?

There’s a decent chance you’re reading this on something that has a few, which is wild to think! Many laptops use thin copper heat pipes to draw heat away from the processor.

A heat pipe is basically a closed metal tube with a splash of liquid trapped inside. Warm up one end, and the liquid boils; the vapor rushes to the far end, dumps its heat and turns back into liquid, and a wick along the inner wall soaks it back to the hot end to start over.

Nothing gets pumped, and that’s a big reason microreactor designers like them. The company describes NuSun as a solid-state, heat-pipe-cooled reactor, meaning the heat pipes are the cooling system. Westinghouse built its eVinci microreactor around heat pipes too, and a scaled-down eVinci core went critical in Nevada this summer.

If the pipes can’t carry heat as the computer models predict, the whole design has a problem. So they’re arguably the most important thing to test before anyone loads fuel.

We don’t know how hot this furnace will run yet. NuCube has said in the past that its reactor design can produce heat above 1,800 degrees Fahrenheit, but its October 6 announcement doesn’t specify a temperature for these tests.

The furnace puts out a fraction of NuSun’s power

USREL’s furnace is rated at 250 kilowatts. A Tesla V3 Supercharger peaks at 250 kilowatts too, if you want something to picture. The startup’s website lists NuSun at up to 15 megawatts, or 60 times the furnace’s 250 kilowatts.

So as far as I can tell, the furnace is standing in for a slice of a NuSun core, and the company hasn’t said how many heat pipes will go in.

I couldn’t find the furnace’s size, weight, or maker in anything published so far. The startup’s website doesn’t list NuSun’s dimensions either, other than to say it’s compact enough to travel by road or rail. Seems like something I keep running into.

The heat will feed hydrogen and power-generation tests

The upgraded furnace will also double as a test bed for industrial processes, according to the release, which names hydrogen production, chemical manufacturing, and electricity from a supercritical carbon dioxide Brayton cycle.

That last one’s a mouthful, but it’s basically the same cycle a jet engine runs (squeeze a gas, heat it, let it spin a turbine), with the gas going around a sealed loop instead of out the back. Here, the gas is carbon dioxide pushed past about 1,070 psi and 88 degrees Fahrenheit, where it starts acting like something between a gas and a liquid and can spin a turbine that’s a lot smaller than a steam turbine doing that job.

USREL already has a pilot-scale supercritical CO2 loop on site, according to the lab’s website, so it isn’t starting from scratch on that front.

NuCube CEO Cristian Rabiti said in the release that the new setup will allow “meaningful validation of energy-conversion and industrial-heat applications.” Translated from press-release English, the company wants to know whether the heat gets where it’s supposed to go and whether it does anything useful once it’s there.

A federal earmark is covering the upgrade

Utah’s Office of Energy Development, which owns and operates USREL, is allocating a $1.35 million Department of Energy award to the furnace work and two other projects. The money is congressionally directed spending, which is the Senate’s polite name for an earmark, and the state thanks Utah Sen. John Curtis for his support.

OxEon Energy, the Utah company whose electrolysis hardware rode to Mars on NASA’s Perseverance rover, gets $620,000 of it for those two projects. The rest goes to BYU and NuCube for the furnace upgrades.

That’s furnaces, plural. The upgrade money also covers the lab’s L-1500 coal furnace, which the state lists at 1 megawatt, or four times the induction furnace’s 250 kilowatts.

The lab’s street address is on Coal Haul Road, in the middle of Utah’s coal country. There’s something a little poetic about one federal check paying to fix up a coal furnace and a fake nuclear core at one lab.

USREL has already had a real reactor go critical

If the lab’s name rings a bell, it’s probably because Valar Atomics took its Ward 250 reactor critical there on June 18, under a federal program meant to get new test reactors running fast. We covered that one when it went critical inside a tent in the Utah desert.

Going critical just means the chain reaction is keeping itself going. The Ward 250 run was a zero-power test, according to the Department of Energy, so it showed the core could sustain a chain reaction without making useful heat.

NuCube wants a real reactor at USREL eventually, too. It has a memorandum of understanding with the state’s energy office to work toward installing one of its microreactors at the lab, and minutes from Utah’s Energy Research Board describe the end goal as a fueled test reactor on-site.

An MOU is basically a written promise to try. Most of this one isn’t legally binding. It runs for 24 months, through May 2027, unless the two sides replace it with a definitive agreement before then.

The company is also partway through going public. In June, it agreed to merge with Launch Two Acquisition Corp., a SPAC (basically a shell company already on the stock market that exists to buy a private company), and the two filed their registration statement with the SEC in September. The deal hasn’t closed yet.

Utah’s energy office announced the federal award on October 5, a day before the startup’s release, and it says the upgraded furnaces will be there to test “a range of energy technologies.” So NuCube’s heat pipes probably won’t be the only thing cooking in Orangeville.

text:
Ford Lightning pickups. (Ford Motor Co.)

It turns out, to make Ford Motor’s electric pickup truck a sales champion, the company just had to stop making it.

Since the final F-150 Lightning rolled off the assembly line in December, it has become one of the most coveted cars in America and a glowing ember in the red-hot market for used electric vehicles. The surging demand shows that there is plenty of appetite for electric trucks among U.S. drivers, provided the pickups aren’t too expensive, said Jimmy Douglas, CEO of Plug, a wholesale electric vehicle dealer.

READ MORE: Toyota RAV4s are the most coveted used cars in America

“When Ford was selling it brand new, the math was complicated,” Douglas said. “But used, the Lightning is 50% to 60% of the sticker price and that is really a sweet spot; it’s an incredible truck for the money.”

In addition to being put off by high prices, truck drivers have been relatively slow to go electric because the machines aren’t very aerodynamic. The boxy build and hefty weight of a half-ton pickup hamstring driving range. However, combustion trucks fight the same physics when it comes to mileage. Pickup fans, in short, have felt the sting of the high gas prices, spiked by the Iran war, more keenly than most drivers.

Scarcity has helped too. In a good year, Ford sells about 900,000 gas-powered F-150s, whereas it moved slightly more than 100,000 of its electric version in a little over four years.

The typical Lightning is changing hands in about 20 days in the U.S., versus 44 days for the average used vehicle. The price has steadily risen to $50,000, an increase of 4% since the start of the year, according to Edmunds.com.

And nearly one-third of used Lightnings are being sold by dealerships that peddle other brands. Typically, those stores would flip a used Ford to a Ford dealer, according to Douglas, but many are electing to list the car directly to tap red-hot demand.

Chase Norris, a county planner in Colorado ski country, recently ditched his gas F-150 for a used Lightning. At $40,000, he considered the vehicle both a major upgrade and a bargain.

“It’s better for the environment and it happens to be faster than some Mustangs,” Norris said. “And I go camping a lot; if it gets cold at night I can just plug my electric blanket into the outlet.”

Part of the appeal for customers like Norris, however, is they won’t notice much of a difference. The exterior of the Lightning is pretty much identical to the gas-powered version — so is the cabin, right down to the massive gear selector, which folds down into the center console. The only apparent EV exception is the yawning front trunk where the spark plugs and cylinders used to be. In a pinch, the truck can also power a house.

Ford’s straightforward bet with the Lightning was that EV buyers were simply drivers who wanted a vehicle that was quieter, easier on the environment and cheaper to fuel and maintain. “One of the best things Ford could have done,” Douglas said, “is making the F-150 Lightning look like an F-150.”

The problem, according to analysts, is that Ford never really delivered on its promise to sell its battery-powered pickup at prices in line with its gas trucks. The $40,000 window sticker trumpeted at the vehicle launch was quickly scrubbed off and replaced by $50,000. Even that number was seldom evident on dealership lots. In its first year of sales, the average transaction price on an F-150 Lightning — what buyers actually paid — was $79,000, because Ford made a greater share of fancier, higher-priced iterations of the vehicle, according to Edmunds.com. Meanwhile, gas F-150s were going for $19,000 less on average. Even at those levels, Ford was losing heaps of money on its EVs, at one point more than $100,000 for each unit sold.

On the used market, however, Lightning prices are comparable to those of gas-powered F-150s. At parity, it appears customers like the EV version as much or more than the traditional machine, at least when gas prices are dear.

The EV Group, which sells pre-owned battery-powered vehicles nationwide from three dealerships, has seen a lot of customers buying Ford Lightnings as a second truck. They drive the electric rig during the weekly commute and fire up the gas model on weekends, according to EV Group CEO and cofounder Alex Lawrence.

“When you do the math on how much they’re going to save,” Lawrence said, “sometimes the used EV is free, if that makes sense.”

At the moment, though, Lawrence’s lots are Lightning free. Even though his stores are selling about 300 vehicles a month, he can’t get his hands on any used electric F-150s — at least not at the right price.

Ultimately, Ford’s decision to kill the Lightning was part of an aggressive retooling of its entire EV strategy. The company set up a new skunkworks in California to make an affordable electric truck — and to do so efficiently enough to also turn a profit.

Next year, Ford promises an all-new electric pickup, dubbed Fathom, with a starting sticker price around $28,000. Although Lightning sales never topped 34,000 a year, Ford hopes to sell 100,000 of the new pickups annually. Kevin Roberts, director of market intelligence at CarGurus Inc., a digital sales platform, said recent demand for used Lightnings bodes well for Fathom sales.

“Used EV demand has shown customers are willing to consider electric when the value proposition is right,” Roberts said. “Ford’s announced [sticker price] puts the Fathom directly into that affordability conversation.”

Ford declined to comment, but has acknowledged that getting EV economics tuned for both profit and low prices remains a tough exercise. At a conference last week, Ford CEO Jim Farley said the company “hasn’t landed the plane yet” on mass production of its new EV platform.

“It’s going to be a heck of an effort,” he explained, “to launch this at scale, at cost, on time.”
