title: Losing the Endangerment Finding: The Costs and Benefits of Repealing Greenhouse Gas ...
description:
In September 2026, EPA repealed the 2024 standards limiting greenhouse gas emissions from power plants under Section 111(d) of the Clean Air Act and proposed the repeal of all remaining greenhouse gas emission requirements for power plants.
In this blog post, we offer a fresh perspective and evaluate the economic and environmental outcomes of repealing the 2024 standards regulating power plant greenhouse gas emissions established under Section 111(d) of the Clean Air Act.
A rollback scenario built directly on the baseline scenario that also includes the repeal of the power plant greenhouse gas standards.
Our upcoming report will provide additional details about how the repeal of vehicle greenhouse gas standards will affect the power sector.
Greenhouse Gas Damages Are Substantial However, the system cost savings from the rollback are dramatically offset by the greenhouse gas damages that the rollback causes—we estimate these greenhouse gas damages to amount to nearly $1.7 trillion.
text:
The rescission of the endangerment finding in February of this year by the US Environmental Protection Agency (EPA) started a cascade of deregulatory actions that have dramatically changed the landscape of climate and air-pollution regulations. In September 2026, EPA repealed the 2024 standards limiting greenhouse gas emissions from power plants under Section 111(d) of the Clean Air Act and proposed the repeal of all remaining greenhouse gas emission requirements for power plants.

EPA argues that the increase in greenhouse gas emissions due to this rollback will have a minimal impact on public health and welfare; as a result, EPA contends, these emissions do not warrant regulation by the agency, and the forgone climate benefits of the repeal can be ignored in EPA’s accompanying regulatory impact analyses. The impact analyses performed by EPA also do not account for the public health impacts of criteria air pollutants such as sulfur dioxide and particulate matter, contradicting guidelines from the Office of Management and Budget and EPA itself.

Ignoring emissions of greenhouse gases and criteria air pollutants goes against decades of scientific peer review and best practice for benefit-cost analysis. Because EPA does not account for the economic costs and benefits of carbon emissions or local air pollution, the agency’s reported cost savings do not reflect the true impact of the regulatory rollback.

This dramatic departure from best practices became especially problematic when EPA updated other parts of its regulatory impact analysis for the final rule. The agency assumed significant growth in electricity demand from data centers, the phaseout of the Inflation Reduction Act’s clean energy tax credits, and a changing electricity generation mix with notably more coal capacity. As a result of these assumption changes made in the final rule, EPA estimates that repealing the regulation on power plants will save approximately $280 billion in compliance costs (minus transfers such as tax payments and credits) between now and 2047, versus estimated savings of $53 billion in the proposed rule.

It follows that emissions of greenhouse gases and air pollutants increase under the final rule’s updated analysis, as higher electricity demand translates to greater capacity and generation needs which are met in part by coal and other fossil fuels. EPA’s decision to ignore the damages from these emissions means that its new analysis tells a story of increasing cost savings without acknowledging the increasing health and climate damages caused by the repeal. We estimate these damages to be many times larger than these cost savings.

In this blog post, we offer a fresh perspective and evaluate the economic and environmental outcomes of repealing the 2024 standards regulating power plant greenhouse gas emissions established under Section 111(d) of the Clean Air Act. We find that the forgone benefits from the repeal outweigh the cost savings by almost $1.5 trillion between 2032 and 2050, even before accounting for the effects of air pollution–related health damages.

Model and Scenarios

We use the power sector model E4ST to estimate how repealing the power plant standards affects the electricity generation mix, decisions over power plant investment and retirement, power-sector emissions, and system-level grid costs. We will quantify the health damages from increased air-pollutant emissions in a future blog post and in our final report.

In this analysis, we evaluate the impacts of rolling back these standards under two scenarios:

A baseline scenario that incorporates all federal and state regulations and policies on the books as of February 2026, including the repeal of the greenhouse gas rules for light-duty vehicles, the One Big Beautiful Bill Act amendments to the clean energy tax credits of the Inflation Reduction Act, and the repeal of the Good Neighbor Plan (which is currently stayed).

A rollback scenario built directly on the baseline scenario that also includes the repeal of the power plant greenhouse gas standards.

In both scenarios, we use demand growth projections that reflect a rapidly changing power sector with significant increases in electricity demand driven by data center growth.

Our upcoming report will provide additional details about how the repeal of vehicle greenhouse gas standards will affect the power sector. While in our baseline and rollback scenario we account for these effects (namely reduced electricity demand from electric vehicles, which causes some changes in grid mix and slightly reduced US power-sector emissions), we do not discuss them in detail here; instead, we focus on the more significant grid effects of the rolled-back power plant standards.

Coal Plants Remain Online

The effects of the rollback on grid resources and the generation mix are accompanied by shifts in both capital expenditures and operating costs. The national average wholesale electricity price is $0.84–$2.00 per megawatt-hour lower in the power plant rollback scenario than in the baseline scenario, which is roughly a 3 to 7 percent reduction. Electricity prices are lower under the rollback scenario primarily for two reasons: First, the power plant rules limit how often new natural gas units can run, making them a more expensive resource. Second, coal units with CCS cost more to run than unretrofitted units.

Our modeling projects that the rollback would reduce total system costs incurred by electric power producers, which are ultimately passed on to consumers through electricity bills. We estimate the change in total system costs as the difference in compliance cost minus transfers, or the sum of capital expenditures, operating costs, and fuel costs between the two scenarios. Using a 3 percent discount rate, the rollback yields a net present value of $221 billion in system savings (in 2024 dollars) between 2032 and 2050, discounted to 2026.

These savings stem primarily from lower capital expenditures by power producers, as retaining paid-off coal capacity under the rollback scenario reduces the need for investment in new grid resources. Operational costs also fall, because retrofitted coal units (required by the power plant rules) have higher variable and fixed costs than unretrofitted coal units.

Greenhouse Gas Damages Are Substantial

However, the system cost savings from the rollback are dramatically offset by the greenhouse gas damages that the rollback causes—we estimate these greenhouse gas damages to amount to nearly $1.7 trillion. We arrive at this figure using the modeled change in carbon dioxide emissions from the rollback, the social cost of carbon, and a 2 percent discount rate consistent with the Office of Management and Budget’s 2023 guidelines. On net, repealing the standards harms society by almost $1.5 trillion, even before accounting for health damages from the widespread deterioration of air quality, which especially affect areas with higher unretrofitted coal-fired generation. We will provide estimates of these public health damages in an upcoming blog post and in our final report.

Electricity demand is rapidly rising in the United States due to electrification trends and data center growth. This increasing demand, and the mix of resources that energy producers use to meet that demand, will meaningfully influence the cost savings and forgone climate and air-quality benefits of the rollback of power plant greenhouse gas standards. If these trends continue, failing to account for the effects of regulatory rollbacks on air pollution and climate change will increasingly misrepresent the net benefits of regulations and downplay their role in protecting Americans and the rest of the world from detrimental health and climate damages.

text:
Conservative Leader Pierre Poilievre pulled up to Dieppe Gardens on Windsor's riverfront Tuesday morning in a Windsor-built Chrysler Pacifica ahead of meetings in Detroit, where he'll continue to pitch a new auto pact.

Poilievre was in Windsor back in March too for similar meetings in the U.S., but he told reporters the environment has changed dramatically since then.

"The situation is much more dire. Back in March we thought we were going to imminently have a deal. Since that time, there has been no deal. The tariffs have worsened, and now there's the threat of a massive tariff increase on January 1," said Poilievre. "Those threats are already paralyzing investments on the Canadian side of the border."

(Photo of Conservative Leader Pierre Poilievre with MP Harb Gill, MP Dave Epp, MP Chris Lewis, and MP Kathy Borelli by Adelle Loiselle)

Conservative MPs Kathy Borrelli, Chris Lewis, Harb Gill and David Epp will join Poilievre at meetings with officials at the International Brotherhood of Electrical Workers, General Motors, and the Ford Rouge Complex.

Poilievre again pitched that a Conservative government would incentivize and lower the price of a new vehicle made in Canada by removing the GST.

"Make it easier to buy Canadian. We as Conservatives are proposing to take the GST off Canadian-made automobiles, which would reduce the cost of a Canadian-made car in Canada by five per cent," said Poilievre, adding that it would incentivise the production of 30,000 more vehicles in this country."

He also proposed removing subsidies to buy electric vehicles and removing "the backdoor" EV mandate.

Poilievre noted that for every ten vehicles made in Canada, nine are sold in the U.S. He said an auto pact could reverse declines in auto production since 2015.

The auto pact, as proposed by the Conservative Leader, would allow Canada and the U.S. to produce more vehicles without tariffs.

"The more an automaker produces in Canada, the more it can sell in Canada. The more it makes in the U.S., the more it could sell in the U.S.," said Poilievre. "For Canada, that would mean production could grow by 500- to 800,000 automobiles over the next ten years."

While Poilievre continued to criticize the Carney Liberals for their handling of the trade war on this side of the border, he pledged to back them on the U.S. side.

"That means putting country ahead of party, and that is what Conservatives will do," he pledged.

title: Solar industry spends to flip control of Georgia utility commission - Canary Media
description:
But Georgia is one of the only states that could flip party control of its public utility commission, an often overlooked institution that determines how much people’s energy bills will rise.
It also touches on the combustible topic of data center construction, as utility Georgia Power seeks to build massive new fossil-gas plants to serve AI customers in the state.
Now, the solar industry is hoping to sway the outcome for the candidates more supportive of clean energy deployment — in this case, the Democrats.
As for the potential rewards, Georgia stands at the precipice of massive new grid investment, making the next few years crucial for determining what Georgia Power builds.
If the Democrats flip control of the PSC, SEIA could build credibility in its effort to spend dollars sparingly but effectively.
text:
Voters will have a chance to pick their utility regulators in nine states this November. But Georgia is one of the only states that could flip party control of its public utility commission, an often overlooked institution that determines how much people’s energy bills will rise.

Last year, as energy affordability bubbled to the surface of the American political scene, Democrats won two of the five seats on the previously all-Republican Georgia Public Service Commission, which oversees utilities’ spending and how much those companies can charge their captive customers. One of those new commissioners — Peter Hubbard — has to run again this year due to a quirk of scheduling. Another Democrat, Shelia Edwards, is running for an open seat on the commission.

The race has attracted attention from advocates and wonks who follow utility regulation and consumer protection. It also touches on the combustible topic of data center construction, as utility Georgia Power seeks to build massive new fossil-gas plants to serve AI customers in the state. Now, the solar industry is hoping to sway the outcome for the candidates more supportive of clean energy deployment — in this case, the Democrats.

A super PAC tied to the Solar Energy Industries Association is spending $250,000 to run ads on behalf of Hubbard and Edwards, on digital platforms and connected TV, like streaming services.

That’s a slight sum compared to, say, the $77.6 million that has been spent on Georgia’s U.S. Senate race. But it’s also the solar trade group’s largest investment in an election in the aftermath of a bruising policy loss in last year’s congressional budget law, which ended up slashing tax credits for renewable energy despite the industry’s lobbying. Emerging from that fight, SEIA took a ​“hard look” at what it needed to do to build durable political power, said Steph Bosh, the organization’s senior vice president of communications.

The solar industry has grown from a power-sector sideshow to a driving force in the last 20 years. But it has yet to build a political operation to compete with the likes of incumbent fossil-fuel lobbies. To help rectify this, Bosh took the helm at SEIA’s 501(c)(4) nonprofit, the Community Clean Energy Coalition, and raised $2 million from industry and philanthropic sources to disburse through its affiliated American Power Forward PAC in this cycle.

Meanwhile, a separate group of clean energy investors and entrepreneurs recently launched the Invest in Tomorrow Coalition PAC, a truculent effort to exact electoral revenge on politicians who led the charge against clean energy policies in last year’s federal budget process. In the primary cycle this year, the coalition batted a perfect score: Five of its targets lost their races, while a pro-renewables Republican the PAC supported won hers. This month, the PAC announced a new slate of targets for the general election, committing $15 million to hounding them with negative ads.

SEIA has kept its distance from that effort, with CEO Tim Pawlenty previously telling Canary Media that his group is ​“in the business of making more friends, not more enemies.” SEIA’s involvement in the Georgia race reveals a more nuanced strategic orientation: Engage in elections where the smallest check can produce the biggest benefit for clean energy.

“If you’ve got one or two million, you need to spend that money really wisely. And so it’s not our goal to be everywhere across the whole country,” Bosh said. SEIA analyzed where politicians were getting in the way of clean energy, then looked for tight vote margins and levels of election spending that were more approachable, ​“so that if we had a limited amount of resources, we knew where we could actually move the needle the furthest.”

Public utility commission races don’t attract the kind of money and attention that congressional races or higher-ranking statewide contests do. A few hundred thousand dollars could make a dent, and with such low general awareness of the race, simply letting voters know it’s happening can help.

As for the potential rewards, Georgia stands at the precipice of massive new grid investment, making the next few years crucial for determining what Georgia Power builds.

On one realistic extreme, the utility could tally up all the proposed data centers that tech giants say they want to build in the state, and then construct as many gas turbines as it would take to provide that new capacity.

However, if the regulators overseeing the utility had a more critical mindset, they could push for a higher share of cheap solar generation paired with batteries as part of the portfolio. Gas turbines keep getting more expensive, and their timelines for delivery keep stretching further into the future, but solar and storage together offer a low-cost and relatively quick-to-build alternative. This approach could protect consumers from the inflationary pressure on gas power plants by locking in stable, fuel-free electricity sources.

If voters are skeptical that the current Public Service Commission majority has their pocketbooks firmly in mind, it may be because they’ve familiarized themselves with the PSC’s recent activity.

The body has approved six utility requests to raise customer rates since 2023, SEIA noted. Last December, the commission responded to the surprise Democratic wins by passing, on the eve of the new commissioners’ swearing-in, a sweeping approval for Georgia Power to build 10 gigawatts of new gas plants and batteries in anticipation of data center demand, raising average household bills by an estimated $20 per month.

Then there’s the case of Republican Tricia Pridemore, who resigned from her commission seat on Sept. 4 and, before the dust could settle in her old office, began lobbying for DC Blox, one of the largest AI infrastructure developers operating in Georgia. (Pridemore told The Georgia Recorder that she won’t appear at the commission on behalf of her new employer, at least for the first year, a time frame stipulated by Georgia’s revolving-door policy.)

If the Democrats flip control of the PSC, SEIA could build credibility in its effort to spend dollars sparingly but effectively. ​“Our goal is to raise a lot more in the future,” Bosh said.

title: The Bizarre Sales Success That Is The Discontinued Ford F-150 Lightning EV
description:
The Ford F-150 Lightning is a curious vehicle.
The Best Proof That The EVs Are Just Too Damn Expensive I don’t think I’ve driven an F-150 Lightning, but I remember David rraving about it when it first appeared on the market.
Given that the F-150 Lightning was initially priced at a level somewhat competitive with gas-powered trucks, it seemed possible that the Lightning could have been a hit.
If this is a good sign for anyone, it’s Ford itself, which is about to reveal the much cheaper Ford Fathom electric pickup truck.
Per the Detroit Free Press: The incumbent UAW president claimed victory in a news release late Friday, Oct. 9.
text:
The Ford F-150 Lightning is a curious vehicle. Engineered to basically be an F-150 with an electric motor, it was a good faith effort at shortcutting its way into the electric truck market. It didn’t quite work as planned, and an ill-timed fire at the automaker’s aluminum supplier basically doomed the slow-selling Lightning. Now that Ford isn’t making them, they’re in high demand.

Today is, obviously, the 10th anniversary of the knighting of Rod Stewart, so I might keep The Morning Dump a little briefer than usual.

While used Lightnings are selling well, new BMWs continue to dominate the luxury market in the United States. The UAW ticket led by Shawn Fain absolutely cleaned up in elections, so I should talk about that. And China and the EU have come to a deal on hybrids.

The Best Proof That The EVs Are Just Too Damn Expensive

I don’t think I’ve driven an F-150 Lightning, but I remember David rraving about it when it first appeared on the market. This was a vehicle that made a lot of compromises in order to share parts with the normal F-150, which wasn’t a bad strategy. Given that the F-150 Lightning was initially priced at a level somewhat competitive with gas-powered trucks, it seemed possible that the Lightning could have been a hit.

Relative to other electric trucks, the Lightning did well, it’s just that there wasn’t enough demand for new electric trucks that cost upwards of $60,000. Even when Ford lowered the cost of the Lightning it wasn’t enough to stoke sufficient volume to offset all the money the company was losing building them.

When Ford’s main aluminum supplier caught on fire (twice), the resulting shutdown hit F-150 production hard, and the company prioritized profitable gas pickup trucks over unprofitable EVs, eventually killing the Lightning.

Now that you can no longer buy a new Lightning (unless one is hiding on a lot somewhere), the truck is suddenly extremely popular. As my old buddy Kyle Stock reports, it’s Lightning Time:

The typical Lightning is changing hands in about 20 days in the U.S., versus 44 days for the average used vehicle. The price has steadily risen to $50,000, an increase of 4% since the start of the year, according to Edmunds.com.

And nearly one-third of used Lightnings are being sold by dealerships that peddle other brands. Typically, those stores would flip a used Ford to a Ford dealer, according to Douglas, but many are electing to list the car directly to tap red-hot demand.

Chase Norris, a county planner in Colorado ski country, recently ditched his gas F-150 for a used Lightning. At $40,000, he considered the vehicle both a major upgrade and a bargain.

This is the best evidence yet for there being some demand for electric vehicles once you knock a few percentage points off the cost. The running costs are also probably much lower if you can charge at home and avoid expensive gas.

If this is a good sign for anyone, it’s Ford itself, which is about to reveal the much cheaper Ford Fathom electric pickup truck.

BMW’s Pretty Good Year

BMW is the one German automaker I think is doing it generally right. I know that not everyone is on board with every decision the brand makes. As an E39 owner I have feelings about new BMWs. Those feelings are never sadness or disgust, however. And when I get to drive one I remember how much I still enjoy them.

That’s showing up in sales, with BMW extending its overall lead in the luxury space with more than 100,000 sales in Q3, which is a little more than Lexus (93k), and Mercedes-Benz (76k). Audi sales aren’t out yet, though it’s clear they’ll still be low.

How’s the brand doing it? Here are some details via Automotive News:

“Our dealers and our brand continue to buck the trend of what’s happening in the premium space overall,” Tom Shanley, BMW of North America’s executive vice president of operations, told Automotive News.

U.S. sales of the 3 Series jumped 46 percent to 11,256 in the third quarter.

“That’s one of our most affordable vehicles for an entry point in the premium space,” Shanley said. “That really drove some additional performance.”

The market for luxury crossovers and SUVs continues to be robust, Shanley said, with the BMW X3, X5, X6 and X7 each posting gains in the third quarter. BMW dealers will receive a key product this month with the launch of the redesigned X5 crossover.

Good, reasonably (for what they are) priced cars, across a large range of segments, isn’t a bad way to do it.

Shawn Fain Easily Wins Four More Years As UAW President

United Auto Workers President Shawn Fain’s hard-nosed tactics helped his union win historic contracts with automakers. Those same tactics seem to be a little more problematic within the union, with the court-appointed monitor singling out Fain for retaliating against people who disagreed with him or he didn’t like.

Members of the UAW didn’t seem to be bothered by the alleged transgressions.

Per the Detroit Free Press:

The incumbent UAW president claimed victory in a news release late Friday, Oct. 9. Fain was overwhelmingly reelected by UAW members in the union’s leadership elections, securing the post with over 68% of the vote. Rich Boyer, the UAW’s current vice president who has been at odds with Fain for years, came in second place with just over 13% of the vote. In total, nearly 100,000 votes were cast.

It is a striking referendum on the popularity of Fain, who led the union through widely publicized strikes against the Detroit Three automakers in 2023 just months after taking office for the first time. Fain has catapulted into the political circuit, too, becoming a common figure at rallies for pro-labor Democrat politicians and candidates.

Success is alluring.

EU Limits Hybrid Imports

The EU was so laser focused on Chinese EVs it sort of forgot to regulate Chinese hybrids. It sounds like resolution to this issue is coming, with the European Union restricting hybrids to 350,000 imported per year. In theory, this applies to everyone, in practice, this is about Chinese cars.

Still, that’s a lot of cars, and a victory for Chinese automakers. What does the EU get out of it?

As Bloomberg reports:

In parallel, China will remove tariffs on some auto parts and halve duties for shoes, ice-cream and olive oil, the document says. Those moves, which will also apply temporarily, would cover about €4 billion worth of exports.

The two sides will also discuss ways to ease export controls and licenses, in particular regarding the supply of rare earths and permanent magnets, according to the document. The EU and China also agreed to exchange more information on their respective export restrictions.

Ice cream! Olive Oil!

What I’m Listening To While Writing TMD

Well, now that I said it, here’s Sir Rod Stewart with “Young Turks.” Young hearts, be free tonight.

The Big Question

What’s the best used EV deal right now?

text:
Xcimer Energy: One of two companies in the DOE Milestone Program working on an inertial confinement concept, Xcimer announced that it has finalized an agreement to receive as much as $30.5 million in additional Milestone Program funding after it successfully completes and receives independent verification of certain preagreed technical and commercialization achievements.

Those achievements are linked to the company’s development of an excimer laser system for a commercial fusion power plant. Instead of using large numbers of solid-state laser beams and costly optical components, as in conventional approaches to inertial fusion, Xcimer’s system is based on “cost-effective gas lasers, durable gas optics, and a two-beamline configuration designed to deliver megajoule-scale laser energy repeatedly and economically,” according to the company.

Xcimer cofounder and CEO Conner Galloway said of the new funding agreement, “We have moved from proving that the physics works to building the industrial technology that can turn fusion into a commercial energy source. This additional milestone funding gives us another powerful mechanism to accelerate that work while keeping the majority of the investment and risk in the private sector.”

The company hopes to have its excimer laser-based fusion system ready to deliver electricity to the grid by the mid-2030s. It previously announced several developments this year as it advances its laser fusion architecture and expands its high-energy laser development programs toward that goal.

In June, for example, Xcimer launched the operation of its Phoenix prototype system, which it described as “the world’s largest privately owned laser system, which demonstrates key elements of Xcimer’s excimer-laser and gas-optics architecture.” Also in June, the DOE approved the preconceptual design and technology road map milestones for the company’s commercial power plant architecture, Athena.

Zap Energy: One of two companies in the DOE Milestone Program developing “innovative” power plant concepts that do not fit into established fusion confinement categories, Zap announced DOE approval of two capacitor development milestones: a pulsed power capacitor designed for the repetition rate and operating lifetime of a fusion power plant and a first prototype capacitor designed, manufactured, and tested entirely at the company. According to Zap, achievement of these two milestones demonstrates “progress in both long-life capacitor design and the U.S.-based manufacturing capabilities needed to produce these components at scale.”

The company has been developing a type of pulsed-power fusion technology that it calls sheared-flow-stabilized Z-pinch, which it says “uses pulses of electrical current to compress a plasma column approximately 50 centimeters long. As the plasma compresses, carefully controlled axial flow stabilizes the pinch, enabling the temperatures and pressures required for fusion.”

The newly approved pulsed-power capacitor design consists of a 35-kV, actively-cooled capacitor that is rated for 50,000 amps of peak current and is projected to continue functioning for 6 billion pulses. According to Zap, the capacitor “uses self-healing metallized polypropylene film, which degrades gradually rather than failing outright, and places several capacitor sections in series inside each winding so the film sees only a small fraction of the terminal voltage.”

The DOE-approved prototype is a compact, 2.8-pound epoxy-potted capacitor designed with the same multisection winding approach used for the other approved capacitor. Developed, assembled, and tested in-house, it was cycled hundreds of times at 8 kV and at more than 7,000 amps, and its capacitance held steady to within 0.25 percent across the full test campaign.

Zap CEO Zabrina Johal noted that “commercial fusion requires more than achieving fusion conditions. It requires the technologies around the fusion core to operate reliably, repeatedly, and at power plant scale. Pulsed power is one of those critical enabling technologies. These milestones demonstrate progress toward the long-life, high-repetition-rate systems a commercial fusion plant will need while building the manufacturing capability to produce them here in the United States.”

Commonwealth Fusion Systems: CFS is one of the companies participating in the DOE Milestone Program as a magnetic confinement tokamak fusion developer. It reports that the DOE has selected it as the only private company to lead a project in the government’s Genesis Mission, which is using partnerships between national laboratories, industry, and academia to apply artificial intelligence to energy generation, scientific research, and national security.

The CFS-led project is focused on the development of an AI-enabled digital twin platform to optimize the operations of the company’s SPARC prototype fusion machine, which is currently being assembled in Devens, Mass. The company expects SPARC “to achieve the first commercially relevant demonstration of net fusion energy and . . . pave the way for CFS to build and optimize ARC [SPARC’s planned successor] commercial fusion power plants,” it said.

The project will involve the use of DOE supercomputers to process fusion data, strengthen AI tools, and advance digital twin visualization work that was previously started by CFS, Nvidia Corporation, and Siemens. CFS said the project will include “building the software infrastructure to connect to DOE computing resources; building the training datasets and AI surrogate models needed for an AI-enabled digital twin; training reinforcement learning and agentic AI models to be used by an AI-based SPARC operations co-pilot; and building data visualization pipelines that accelerate operations.”

CFS expects the AI-enabled digital twin to help accelerate commercial fusion deployment “by allowing rapid iteration in the SPARC control room.”

CFS cofounder and chief science officer Brandon Sorbom said that the project “will convert decades of R&D performed across the U.S. fusion community into tools that can be applied to accelerate SPARC operations. Together, our team of public and private leaders in AI and fusion will be able to unify and apply decades of U.S. research and tackle some of the fusion industry’s biggest challenges.”

title: Vietnamese entrepreneurs: New opportunities, new mission - Theinvestor.vn
description:
But this new status also poses a more difficult question for Vietnamese entrepreneurs: with a broader scope for development, a changing institutional framework and access to increasingly larger playing fields, are Vietnamese businesses capable of stepping up?
They are becoming increasingly evident in sectors where Vietnamese private businesses previously had limited ability to establish a significant presence.
This is a notable example of Vietnamese businesses shifting from relying on economies of scale to meeting higher industrial standards.
These moves show Vietnamese businesses seeking to advance further into higher-value segments of the technology chain.
Behind Vietnam's enormous export figures, therefore, lies a question about how much value Vietnamese businesses retain.
text:
On the occasion of Vietnam Entrepreneurs’ Day on October 13, journalist Lam Son examines the country’s expectations for a new generation of businesses that can go beyond building substantial wealth for their founders to take part in major national projects, control more critical links in technology value chains, and integrate more deeply into global supply chains.

Never before has the private sector occupied such a prominent position in Vietnam. Once viewed primarily as a supplementary component of the economy, the private sector is now identified as “one most important driver of the national economy” and is expected to become a pioneering force in science-technology, innovation and digital transformation.

The Politburo's Resolution 68 emerged against this backdrop, opening the way for a major shift in roles. But this new status also poses a more difficult question for Vietnamese entrepreneurs: with a broader scope for development, a changing institutional framework and access to increasingly larger playing fields, are Vietnamese businesses capable of stepping up?

If one image were needed to describe the institutional changes since late 2024, it would probably be a vast construction site. The administrative apparatus has been reorganized, the country has moved from 63 to 34 provinces and cities, and a two-tier local government model has been implemented.

At the central level, The Politburo's Resolution 57 on science-technology, innovation and digital transformation; Resolution 59 on international integration; Resolution 66 on lawmaking and law enforcement; and Resolution 68 on private-sector development have been brought together into a framework that Party leaders call the “four pillars”.

These changes converge on one point: creating new room for businesses and entrepreneurs to grow.

From managing to enabling businesses

What stands out first about Resolution 68 is its approach to the private sector. With more than 940,000 businesses and over 5 million household businesses, the sector currently contributes around 50% of GDP, more than 30% of total state budget revenue and employs about 82% of the workforce. By 2030, the target is to have around 2 million businesses, with the private sector contributing 55-58% of GDP and at least 20 large enterprises participating in global value chains.

Policy is consequently beginning to change in more concrete ways. Research and development is one example. Under the National Assembly's Resolution 198/2025/QH15, businesses can deduct research and development expenses at 200% of their actual costs when calculating taxable income. They may also allocate up to 20% of taxable corporate income to funds for developing science-technology, innovation and digital transformation.

For businesses working in semiconductors, artificial intelligence, advanced materials or biotechnology, this represents a significant change. The risks of research remain with businesses, but the state is beginning to share part of the cost of experimentation, a process that always carries the possibility of failure.

Another shift concerns the regulatory approach. Resolution 198 calls for a decisive move from pre-inspection to post-inspection, replacing licensing and certification requirements with declarations of compliance and subsequent inspections in most sectors. In 2026, this requirement is being further translated into measures to cut and simplify administrative procedures and business conditions.

At the local level, the 2025 Provincial Competitiveness Index (PCI) was published for the first time under the PCI 2.0 model following changes to administrative boundaries. Instead of the previous ranking race from first to 63rd place, the 34 provinces and cities were grouped according to the quality of their governance. Bac Ninh, Danang, Hai Phong, Phu Tho and Quang Ninh were placed in the “Good” group.

The new assessment method also reflects a shift in thinking: businesses need a stable environment across multiple dimensions - from access to resources and transparency to compliance costs and legal institutions - rather than a handful of isolated incentives.

This is the foundation of the “new opportunities”. They are becoming increasingly evident in sectors where Vietnamese private businesses previously had limited ability to establish a significant presence.

Infrastructure is one example. Private companies are increasingly involved in large-scale transport projects, from expressways and airports to urban infrastructure. For businesses, entering a national project means moving beyond construction capabilities to managing capital, technology, timelines, safety and responsibility throughout the project's lifecycle.

Hoa Phat is investing more than VND10 trillion ($385.7 million) in a rail and special steel manufacturing plant in Dung Quat (Quang Ngai province), targeting its first high-speed railway rail products in the first quarter of 2027. This is a notable example of Vietnamese businesses shifting from relying on economies of scale to meeting higher industrial standards.

Similar developments are beginning to emerge in core technologies. In early 2026, FPT announced the establishment of an advanced semiconductor chip testing and packaging plant in Bac Ninh city, while continuing to expand its AI Factory infrastructure powered by Nvidia. Viettel has independently designed a 5G digital front-end (DFE) chip and developed a 5G equipment ecosystem. These moves show Vietnamese businesses seeking to advance further into higher-value segments of the technology chain.

New markets are also taking shape rapidly. In 2025, Vietnam's e-commerce market reached around $31 billion, up 25.5%. The target for 2026-2030 is to maintain annual e-commerce retail sales growth of around 20-30%. Alongside the digital economy, carbon markets, green technology, data and new business models supported by controlled regulatory sandboxes are also gaining momentum.

A new garment is being tailored for the private sector. But a larger garment also requires a stronger body.

The doors are open, but bottlenecks remain

At a conference in Ho Chi Minh City in September 2026 to gather feedback on a draft law on small and medium-sized enterprise development, one reality was highlighted: small and medium-sized enterprises account for around 98% of all businesses but only around 20-25% of the economy's total outstanding credit.

This gap cannot be explained simply by banks' reluctance to lend. A significant proportion of businesses still operate as family-run enterprises; business finances and owners' personal finances have not been separated; financial statements lack reliability; risk management is weak; and collateral is limited. When businesses lack transparency, long-term capital is difficult to attract, regardless of how many additional support policies the financial system offers.

The second bottleneck lies in the capacity to participate in value chains. The foreign-invested sector currently contributes more than 20% of GDP and around 70% of export turnover. In the first half of 2026 alone, it accounted for 79.9% of exports, while domestic businesses accounted for just 20.1%.

Behind Vietnam's enormous export figures, therefore, lies a question about how much value Vietnamese businesses retain. A product may be assembled in Vietnam and exported from Vietnam, while its core components, design, technology, brand and distribution network remain elsewhere. The gap between “made in Vietnam” and “value created by Vietnam” remains considerable.

The 2025 PCI introduced the Business Performance Index (BPI) into its assessment system for the first time. The country's median BPI score was only 4.2 out of 10, while the median innovation score was around 4.17. Ho Chi Minh City scored 6.15 for innovation, Hanoi 5.98, while Lam Dong scored just 2.18. The wide disparities between localities show that the private sector's endogenous capabilities remain unevenly developed.

Policy opportunities, therefore, will not automatically translate into business capabilities.

The new mission begins with businesses growing stronger

When Resolution 68 is discussed, much of the focus is on land, credit, administrative procedures, taxes and incentives for innovation. But there is another, less comfortable side to the story: businesses must also change themselves.

The first requirement is better governance. A business seeking large-scale financing, a stock market listing, international capital or participation in projects worth tens of trillions of dong (VND10 trillion = VND385.7 million) cannot continue to operate like an oversized family shop.

Transparent financial statements, independent audits, risk management systems, professional management teams and mechanisms to oversee the exercise of power within companies will increasingly become prerequisites for long-term growth, rather than merely “good standards” reserved for a handful of large corporations.

The second is technology and productivity. The 200% deduction for R&D expenses will only be meaningful if businesses are willing to spend money on research and development. Science and technology funds will create value only when used to develop new products, processes and technologies.

In an economy where the advantage of cheap labor is steadily diminishing, productivity must become a new source of profit. This means moving from contract manufacturing to design, from output volumes to standards, and from selling products to owning technology and brands.

The ST25 rice story offers an illustration. The variety has been named the “World's Best Rice” three times, in 2019, 2023 and 2025. Behind these accolades lie more than three decades of breeding research by engineer Ho Quang Cua and his colleagues. Brand value is ultimately built on science, quality and perseverance, not advertising alone.

Trung Nguyen Legend offers another example. In August 2026, it continued opening Trung Nguyen E-Coffee outlets in Frisco and Garland, Texas. This represents a different approach: taking products overseas together with the story of Vietnamese coffee culture, rather than simply exporting raw materials.

Vietnamese entrepreneurs in this new era must still generate profits. Without profits, businesses cannot survive. But the expectations for a new generation of businesses have grown beyond creating substantial wealth for their founders.

They must also build Vietnamese companies capable of participating in major national projects; gain control of more critical links in technology value chains; integrate domestic businesses more deeply into global supply chains; and create brands whose Vietnamese value is embodied in their products, rather than stopping at the location of their factories.

Resolution 68 sets a target of having at least 20 large enterprises participate in global value chains by 2030. This will be difficult to achieve if millions of businesses remain content with familiar markets, outdated management practices and profits derived from short-term advantages.

The new opportunities are therefore also a test. Institutions must continue to change to safeguard the freedom to do business, ensure equal access to resources, reduce unofficial costs and give businesses that deliver real results the opportunity to grow.

For entrepreneurs, the requirements have also changed. They must become more transparent to attract larger capital flows. They must invest in technology to move into higher-value segments. They must think about global markets from the outset when developing products. More importantly, they must build businesses capable of surviving and thriving across generations rather than depending on a single individual.

text:
On Oct. 1, a coalition of 21 states and the District of Columbia sued the U.S. Environmental Protection Agency (EPA) over its repeal of major greenhouse gas emissions requirements for fossil fuel-fired power plants. The coalition filed the lawsuit in the U.S. Court of Appeals for the D.C. Circuit.

New York Attorney General Letitia James (D) led the challenge, which also includes Pennsylvania Gov. Josh Shapiro (D) and the mayors of New York City and Chicago and the City and County of Denver. The plaintiffs are asking the court to vacate EPA's repeal and restore the previous emissions requirements.

EPA finalized the partial repeal on Sept. 14. The agency eliminated three main parts of the Biden administration's 2024 Carbon Pollution Standards, including emissions guidelines for existing fossil fuel-fired steam-generating units and carbon capture requirements for certain new natural gas-fired power plants.

The states argue that EPA violated the Clean Air Act when it repealed the requirements.

The lawsuit is the latest legal challenge between states and the federal government over the scope of EPA's authority to regulate greenhouse gas emissions from the power sector. The outcome could determine whether EPA must restore major portions of the 2024 standards governing emissions from coal, oil, and natural gas-fired power plants.

The dispute also comes as EPA seeks to eliminate the remaining federal greenhouse gas standards for power plants, including certain efficiency requirements for new and reconstructed natural gas turbines and modified steam-generating units.

The Biden administration finalized the Carbon Pollution Standards in April 2024 under Section 111 of the Clean Air Act. The standards established greenhouse gas emissions requirements for new natural gas-fired power plants and guidelines for states to limit emissions from existing fossil fuel-fired power plants.

On Sept. 14, 2026, EPA Administrator Lee Zeldin announced the partial repeal. The EPA estimated the repeal would save $310 billion across the economy from 2026 through 2047. The agency argues that the changes will reduce regulatory costs and support reliable and affordable electricity.

The states contend that EPA lacks a lawful basis for eliminating the 2024 requirements and are asking the D.C. Circuit to restore the repealed standards.

title: Remanufacturers Get Worn-Out Engines Back to Work
description:

text:
A worn-out heavy-duty engine covered in oily grime is an attractive core that’s in hot demand by engine remanufacturers.

“Even though that engine assembly is non-working, there’s tremendous value in the components and the parts that can be brought back to like-new condition for reuse,” said Kevin Schrag, manager of John Deere Reman, a remanufacturing engine and parts operation for off-highway vehicles.

Heavy-duty engines have been one of the top sectors for remanufacturing activity for many years. “Many factors make heavy-duty engines ideal for remanufacturing. As durable products, the engine and its components are designed to last, and remanufacturing extends the functionality,” said Dr. Nabil Nasr, founder and current board member of the Remanufacturing Industries Council and the CEO of the REMADE Institute.

For today’s engine remanufacturers, the process begins with disassembly of the core. All the disassembled parts undergo an intensive cleaning to remove contaminants. Components are then inspected for wear, damage and defects with needed repairs or replacements made to original equipment specifications. Critical surface areas are precision machined, and dynamic testing confirms that the reassembled core meets or exceeds OEM specifications. A warranty is typically included.

Lifeline for heavy-duty vehicles

A remanufactured John Deere engine – typically 30% cheaper than a new engine – can extend the lifespan of an older agriculture tractor or other off-highway workhorses. John Deere’s remanufacturing work includes more than five decades of engines, including complete 6-cylinder block assemblies of its 4440 tractor produced from 1978-1982.

“We actually run all of the different engine configurations down the same disassembly line and the same assembly line. So that’s very different from our new engine factories that are building two or three sizes of John Deere engines with the latest technology,” Schrag said.

Dozens of different John Deere engine models with displacements ranging from 2.9- to 13.5-L are in the remanufacture mix. “Our engine portfolio continues to grow. And our engine and parts remanufacturing and warehousing footprint has continued to grow,” Schrag said. In 2025, construction began on a 120,000 square foot addition to the John Deere Reman Core Center, one of the firm’s remanufacturing facilities in the Springfield, Missouri region.

The $13.5 million project pushes the reman facility’s footprint to 400,000 square feet in 2026. “One of the challenges that we have is not enough storage space for the core, so this expansion primarily will address that need,” Schrag said. “We start collecting core for several years before we have enough core to start a remanufacture program and sell that remanufactured engine as an off-the-shelf product.” John Deere Reman has more than 500 workers involved with remanufacturing engines and other products for global customers.

Rolls-Royce’s campus in South Carolina substantially strengthened its remanufacturing operations in 2023 with a 69,000 square foot facility expansion. “Under our mtu brand, we manufacture a lot of different engine models for different sectors and applications, so that means there’s a demand for a variety of remanufactured parts and a variety of remanufactured engines,” said Andy Suda, head of service sales for the Americas at Rolls-Royce Solutions America.

The mtu product portfolio provides high-speed engines and propulsion systems for marine applications (including yachts, tugboats and fast ferries), off-road vehicles (including mine hauling trucks and loaders), rail, military vehicles and the oil and gas industry. “Any customer application that runs hard – typically 4,000-plus hours yearly – definitely wants a reman program as their support system because an engine’s mechanical components wear-out and its flexible components breakdown,” Suda said.

There are more than 150,000 mtu-brand engines in operation globally. “We continually release new engine models, so we are making sure that we are positioned appropriately with remanufactured components and remanufactured engines when those first engines wear-out,” Suda said.

The Remanufacturing and Overhaul Center in South Carolina handles remanufacturing tasks for after-sales support with targeted production of 20,000 remanufactured parts a year. “Prior to the expansion, the South Carolina center had a very limited reman scope,” Suda said. “We continue to ramp up our reman capabilities in the U.S. because the demand for reman is growing.”

Decades of reman work

It’s a milestone year for the Volvo Group as the company marks 80 years of remanufacturing components for its on-road, off-road and marine applications. “Our reman business has been growing over the last several years as customers want to use remanufactured product to keep their trucks operating for additional years,” said Sherman Williams, Volvo Group North America’s remanufacturing product development director.

The company offers 3/4 and 7/8 remanufactured engines with the latter picking up steam. “We’re moving our reman business from the lower content product to the higher content 7/8 engine,” Williams said. The 3/4 and 7/8 designations essentially refer to the completeness of the reman engine package. The only components not 7/8 engine-installed are the alternator, starter, fan hub and power steering pump.

“The 7/8 engine allows the end customer to customize the last four pieces of the engine. When an overhaul is needed or it is time to replace the engine, the 7/8’s average installation time savings is one to three days, depending on the application,” Williams said.

Technology improvements are not limited to new engine programs. “We follow the OE specifications and factory guidelines to produce the highest quality Volvo reman engines. Beyond that, if any component has been improved or upgraded – or if a torque spec or a technique has improved over time – we’ll integrate that into our remanufacturing process,” Williams said.

Volvo has hundreds of reman engines in stock. “If there’s a unique application, we can build it in less than 40 days. But most of our reman engines, probably 80%, have off-the-shelf availability,” Williams said.

Reman and the circular economy

Remanufacturing extends the lifespan of products with minimal impact on the environment. “From a sustainability point-of-view, 80 to 90% of the emissions and waste associated with making a product comes from material extraction. There’s a significant environmental value with remanufacturing because manufacturers are using material that’s already been mined and machined. And, there’s significantly lower energy consumption to rework some of the parts versus making new parts,” said Dr. Nasr, who is also the Associate Provost of the Golisano Institute for Sustainability at the Rochester Institute of Technology in New York. When compared to new-product production processes, up to 85% less energy is consumed during remanufacturing processes, which also equates to reduced greenhouse gas emissions.

Components made from iron, steel or aluminum are not the only materials that can be reused. “We remanufacture electronic displays and receivers, but the majority of our electronics work is engine controllers,” said John Deere’s Schrag.

After the unit has been cleaned and diagnostic testing has pinpointed the failure issue, a specialized technician solders in the replacement. “It’s a John Deere designed electronics part, so we know the specs and understand what needs to be replaced. It’s a very detailed process to get it back to like-new condition,” Schrag said. “But the value is the majority of that raw material is something that can be reused, even though there’s more labor put into the task.”

Redesigning reman’s future

There’s an underlying reason why remanufacturing considerations should be an integral part of product development. “If you bring remanufacturing knowledge into the early stage of a new product’s design, that know-how can have a significant impact on the remanufacturing process,” said Dr. Nasr, referencing Phoenix DFR software, a design for remanufacturing tool. Developed by Golisano Institute for Sustainability researchers, this software could shake up the world of design for companies doing both new product manufacturing and remanufacturing.

Over the past few months, many design engineers have been beta testing the Phoenix DFR software with computer-aided design (CAD) plug-ins. “Our initial experience has been positive,” said Jeff Sutherland, Director of Product Management for Caterpillar Remanufacturing.

The new software prompts risk-based design assessments that are exceedingly relevant to remanufacturing work. “Having a software tool that helps a design engineer think through different design decisions is very helpful,” Sutherland said. “Upfront planning means potential issues can be identified in the design stage versus finding out about a problem after the product has been in the field and comes back to us for remanufacturing.”

Remanufactured Caterpillar engines, ranging from 4.4- to 105.8-L displacements for construction and other off-highway applications, are typically 45% to 85% of a new Caterpillar engine’s cost if a used Caterpillar core is remitted. Of course, those end-of-first-life cores are no longer pristine in appearance.

“We get the dirtiest of the dirtiest products coming back to us after the products have been through a useful life,” Sutherland said. The ability to clean a used engine thoroughly is the critical starting point in the remanufacturing process. “A dirty engine can hide a lot of potential issues, so anything that helps us improve the cleaning process is very beneficial,” he said.

Design for remanufacturing software is viewed as a major first step to getting a filthy engine sparkling clean. “There are design features that can be beneficial to the cleaning process, and there are design features that can be detrimental to the cleaning process,” Sutherland said. For instance, concave surfaces on the external casting can trap dirt and debris, “but some of the biggest design problems for cleaning are cross-drilled holes, and blind or hidden passages,” he said.

The Phoenix DFR software can help identify designs that would hinder the cleaning process. “The intent is not to dictate a design. It’s about getting product development engineers to think about potential problems for the remanufacturing process during a new product’s design,” Sutherland said.

Clear communication has always been an effective way to address remanufacturing’s needs. “Even without this software, we spend a lot of time – and I know a lot of other companies spend a lot of time – trying to influence decisions during design reviews, discussions and training. Those are things that are done on an ongoing basis because it’s so important to remanufacturing,” Sutherland said, noting that Caterpillar’s remanufacturing work began in 1973. “This software would further enhance those discussions and remanufacturing processes.”

title: Across the US, people don't want data centers coming to their communities
authors: Neha Gour, John Kotcher, Teresa Myers
description:
Regardless of their views on politics or climate change, most Americans oppose the development of data centers in their communities.
As more data centers are proposed, some local communities are pushing back against new and prospective projects.
Phil Scott vetoed a bill that would have imposed strict regulations on data centers, local governments are taking matters into their own hands by banning data centers in their towns.
Most Americans expect data centers to increase their electricity bills Electricity costs are a major concern Americans have about data centers, particularly amid broader concerns about the increasing cost of living.
As data centers continue to expand across the country, understanding Americans’ views on them, and what people expect from developers, is becoming increasingly important.
text:
Regardless of their views on politics or climate change, most Americans oppose the development of data centers in their communities.

These large buildings filled with computers that store and process digital information, increasingly to support various applications of artificial intelligence, are being built rapidly across the United States. They can bring economic investment and jobs, but the pollution created by generating the electricity they need can also harm public health, pollute air, use up water, create noise and raise energy costs.

As more data centers are proposed, some local communities are pushing back against new and prospective projects. These debates are already influencing local zoning and permitting decisions, and increasingly reaching state lawmakers.

In early September, Massachusetts Gov. Maura Healey issued an executive order that no state agency will issue permits for data center development unless the project already has local approval from the municipality where it will be located. In Vermont, where Gov. Phil Scott vetoed a bill that would have imposed strict regulations on data centers, local governments are taking matters into their own hands by banning data centers in their towns.

Public opinion is playing an important role in shaping how data center expansion unfolds across the country.

We are researchers studying science communication, climate change and public health. To better understand what Americans think about these issues, we examined data from the Spring 2026 Climate Change in the American Mind survey. It is a nationally representative survey of adults in the U.S. conducted by the Yale Program on Climate Change Communication and the George Mason University Center for Climate Change Communication. Our findings align with other recent polling on the topic.

Most Americans oppose a data center in their area

In an April 2026 survey of 1,068 adults, 930 of whom are registered voters, we and our research colleagues Jennifer Carman, Seth Rosenthal, Anthony Leiserowitz and Edward Maibach asked respondents the degree to which they would support or oppose building a data center in their local area.

Just over half – 56% – said they would oppose it, while only 15% said they would support it.

The opposition is not limited to one political group. A majority of Americans in most groups across the political continuum said they oppose the development of data centers in their communities, although the extent of that opposition varies somewhat between groups.

Among registered voters, about three-quarters of liberal Democrats and about half of conservative Republicans said they oppose having a data center built in their local area.

People’s perspectives on climate change

For a closer look at how people view data centers, we built on our past work about Americans’ views about global warming and actions to reduce climate change and its effects. That research has identified six distinct groups of views on those issues, which we call “the Six Americas.”

Opposition to local data centers is highest among those in the Alarmed category, those most worried about climate change – 71% of whom opposed data centers being built in their community. But opposition is also very strong among those in the Dismissive category, who reject the idea that global warming is happening and human-caused.

These findings show that Americans with widely different beliefs about global warming can nonetheless hold similar views about local data center development.

Most Americans expect data centers to increase their electricity bills

Electricity costs are a major concern Americans have about data centers, particularly amid broader concerns about the increasing cost of living. Agreements between power companies and data center owners aren’t always clear about who will pay to generate the massive amounts of electricity involved – and it may be functionally impossible to tell if the costs are shared fairly.

A majority of Americans, 59%, expect their electricity bills to increase if a data center opens in their local area. Just 5% think their bills would decrease; 25% said they don’t know. The remaining 12% said they don’t expect their bills to be affected.

Concern about higher electricity bills is bipartisan. Among registered voters, majorities of every political group expect their bills to increase.

Electricity cost worries also span all views on climate change. The only group where a majority didn’t expect a data center to raise their power bills was the Disengaged, who don’t pay much attention to or hear about climate change very often, of whom 43% reported that expectation. But about as many of that group, 42%, said they didn’t know what might happen to their electric bills.

Most Americans support requiring data centers to offset their electricity use

We also asked Americans about one idea to address the large amount of electricity used by data centers: Instead of building new power plants to provide additional electricity, an advocacy group called Rewiring America has proposed that data center developers could be required to install rooftop solar and help weatherize and insulate nearby homes whose owners want these improvements. Those changes could generate new electricity and save additional energy to help provide the power the data center needs.

Respondents strongly supported making this idea a state or local requirement.

This proposal has considerable public support, from across the political spectrum and among the various Six Americas groups of views on climate change. Only the Dismissive group – those who dismiss the idea that climate change is happening – saw less than half of its members support these policies, even though majorities of that group oppose having a data center nearby and expect a local data center to increase their electricity bills. This is consistent with their tendency to oppose renewable energy development more generally.

What this means

The companies leading the AI boom are seeking not only computer servers, electricity and land, but also public support. As data centers continue to expand across the country, understanding Americans’ views on them, and what people expect from developers, is becoming increasingly important.

Our research shows that Americans with very different political views and opinions about global warming can share similar views about data center development.

Some state regulators and utility companies are already considering structuring electricity rates to prevent data center costs from being passed on to other customers.

At the same time, the differences matter, especially in terms of specific policies that may or may not be broadly popular.

For policymakers, data center developers and community leaders, understanding where different groups agree and disagree can help them better serve the public interest.

text:
TO BE PUBLISHED May 2027

Starting from: £99 + VAT

Format: DOWNLOADABLE PDF

This conference will consider next steps for clean energy investment and delivery in Great Britain, including priorities for mobilising public and private capital, addressing barriers to project development and the role of Great British Energy. Areas for discussion include investment models and commercial viability, infrastructure and grid constraints, UK manufacturing and supply chains, local and community energy, and the implications for jobs, skills and regional economies.

Clean power investment & deployment - public & private capital

It will bring together policymakers and stakeholders to examine priorities for investment and project delivery in the context of Clean Power 2030 ambitions, GBE's Strategic Plan and the wider programme of public investment in clean energy. Delegates will consider the role of public intervention in addressing market barriers, reducing development risks and supporting emerging technologies - as well as the conditions needed to attract private capital and bring projects through to construction and operation. GBE's developing role as an investor, developer and owner of clean energy assets is expected to be a focus of discussion alongside that of the National Wealth Fund and other public and private investment partners.

The conference will examine how effectively public support, commercial investment and local delivery are being coordinated, and assess the effectiveness of these arrangements in delivering additional clean energy capacity, commercially viable projects and wider benefits for UK supply chains, workers and communities.

Investment models, supply chain programmes & delivery partners

The agenda will assess approaches to public and private co-investment, risk allocation, additionality and the commercial sustainability of clean energy projects, including GBE's developing investment model and income-generating portfolio. Discussion will consider the early impact of the Energy, Engineered in the UK programme and its Supply Chain Fund, priorities for strengthening domestic manufacturing and the role of government, the National Wealth Fund, industry and other partners in supporting investment and delivery.

Local power, community ownership & business opportunities

Attendees will look at early implementation of funding and support under the Local Power Plan, including the GBE Community Fund and GBE Partnerships Grant, alongside wider approaches to financing and developing local energy projects. Sessions will consider requirements for scaling commercially sustainable local energy projects, approaches to community ownership - including developing government proposals on shared ownership of renewable projects - and sharing the benefits of clean energy across regions. Opportunities for UK businesses in offshore wind, including floating and other deepwater technologies, electricity networks, hydrogen and emerging clean energy technologies will also be considered.

Grid investment, infrastructure constraints, skills & regional delivery

Further sessions will examine the practical constraints affecting deployment, including grid capacity and connections, network investment, system flexibility and the coordination of generation, storage and demand. Delegates will consider priorities for accelerating electricity network development, the implications of connections reform for project viability and the role of Great British Grid in supporting infrastructure investment and delivery.

Discussion is expected on workforce and skills requirements, the North Sea Future Plan and the role of GBE's Aberdeen Energy Taskforce in supporting regional economic development. Delegates will also assess the effectiveness of public investment arrangements, including questions of commercial discipline, accountability and operational independence, and how progress should be measured against objectives for energy security, public ownership, jobs and industrial capacity, community benefit and long-term value for taxpayers.

Overview of areas for discussion

clean energy investment, additionality & commercial discipline:

investment priorities and emerging project pipelines across offshore, onshore and local energy - public investment and criteria for intervention

co-investment, risk allocation and crowding in private finance - routes from development-stage support to FID and construction - investment certainty and project bankability

risk-weighted returns and portfolio performance - commercial sustainability - GBE's investment model and role alongside other public finance institutions

local & community energy, shared ownership & routes to market:

GBE Community Fund and GBE Partnerships Grant rollout - wider GBE Local grants, loans and development support - pipeline of investable local and community energy projects

scalable and self-sustaining business models - standardised delivery models, access to expertise and finance, and routes to market

shared ownership and community benefit - government proposals and GBE templates for developer-community partnerships - long-term local participation and value from clean energy assets

public sector generation - solar on schools, NHS sites and other public buildings - lessons for scaling and cutting public sector bills

UK manufacturing, supply chains & responsible sourcing:

Energy, Engineered in the UK - Supply Chain Fund for offshore wind and networks - targeting supply chain bottlenecks and areas of UK competitive advantage - leveraging private investment

floating and other deepwater wind, hydrogen, storage and emerging technologies - domestic manufacturing - demand visibility and routes for SMEs

resilience, traceability and due diligence - modern slavery and human-rights risks - ethical standards, deployment pace and affordability

networks, connections & project bankability:

impact of grid capacity and connection times on clean energy investment and project delivery - alignment with connections reform and strategic system planning

coordination with NESO, Ofgem and network companies - sequencing generation, transmission and distribution investment - Great British Grid and opportunities for public-private investment

flexibility and storage - infrastructure constraints affecting project viability, investor confidence and delivery to 2030

workforce transition, skills & regional value:

workforce requirements across development, manufacturing, construction and operations - skills shortages and routes for retraining

North Sea transition - transferability of oil and gas capability - retaining skilled workers and supply chain expertise

GBE Aberdeen Energy Taskforce - converting clean energy investment into local jobs, manufacturing opportunities and regional economic benefit

investment partnerships, governance & measuring impact:

roles of GBE, DESNZ, the National Wealth Fund, devolved governments and other public investment bodies - relationships with private developers and investors - coordination and avoiding duplication

measuring additionality and impact - clean energy capacity, private finance mobilised, jobs, community ownership and supply chain outcomes

operational independence and accountability - DESNZ framework document and leadership beyond the start-up phase - transparency, decision-making, and progress against public investment and clean energy delivery objectives

text:
SINGAPORE – Singapore-based deep-tech company NEU Battery Materials has raised US$7.6 million (S$9.7 million) in an oversubscribed funding round to expand its battery recycling business.

The funding comes after NEU commissioned a new facility in Tuas capable of processing 1,300 tonnes of battery materials a year. The facility marks a major step towards scaling up its operations, although it will not initially run at full capacity.

The company will use the funds to increase production of battery-grade lithium from battery manufacturing scraps and materials from end-of-life batteries, as well as expand overseas.

According to chief executive Bryan Oh, the funds are predominantly allocated to three key areas.

“The first is operating the facility, to help us run the production and collect data,” he said.

“The second is investing significantly in R&D to reduce production costs. Our company’s goal is to become the cheapest source of lithium.”

The third area focuses on expanding the business overseas, specifically in Europe and the US. By partnering with battery manufacturers abroad, NEU aims to scale up its Singapore-designed technology, potentially by five to 10 times, to help countries develop local recycling capabilities.

Oh said localised recycling could help countries secure their lithium supplies and retain greater control over their battery supply chains, given China’s dominance in the lithium supply chain and the lack of natural lithium deposits in Singapore.

The International Energy Agency notes that lithium iron phosphate (LFP) batteries account for over 55% of electric vehicle (EV) batteries and more than 90% of global battery energy storage systems.

According to Oh, mass-market EVs, including models made by BYD, predominantly use LFP batteries due to their lower cost and safety advantages. This makes recycling LFP waste an urgent priority.

“We use an electromechanical redox targeting technology to recycle lithium batteries,” Oh said.

“We specifically focus on recycling LFP and put these waste batteries into our process, and we are able to extract the lithium through an electrolyser to form battery-grade lithium hydroxide, which we then convert to lithium carbonate,” he explained.

He added that the process is unique in three ways: it uses only water and electricity, is highly scalable because of the design of its cells or electrolyser, and is more sustainable than traditional recycling methods.

The facility will not be running at full capacity for now.

“The purpose is to run tests and then improve (the process) so that we can create the final blueprint to replicate for really big scale,” he said.

NEU is working with manufacturers to ensure the recovered lithium meets quality and consistency standards. It is supplying increasingly larger batches for testing, including to some manufacturers that provided the production scrap.

The materials NEU currently receives are mostly manufacturing rejects rather than end-of-life EV batteries . Oh said the company had “future-proofed Singapore for the next decade” by preparing to handle potential increases in EV battery waste.

He noted that the core plant was built to operate at a larger scale and that expanding its capacity to handle thousands of EV batteries would require only minor modifications, such as adding more cells to the electrolyser stack.

This would allow NEU to double its capacity within weeks.

With its scalable recycling model, the company aims to help position Singapore at the forefront of the green transition. Its process generates up to 83% lower carbon emissions than traditional recycling methods, said Oh.
